Breaking: A 100-Foot Fall Stole Her Mobility. Now, Former Climbing Ranger Quinn Brett Is Rebranding Trails for Everyone.

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (919 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Quinn Brett photographed in Chasm Meadows in Rocky Mountain National Park, Colorado (Photo: Courtesy of Brian Watson/Jacob Bailey).
  • Recent findings suggest that in 2017, National Park Service (NPS) climbing ranger Quinn Brett, 36, fell while ascending El Capitan in Yosemite National Park.
  • Like many Americans with mobility disabilities, Brett faced challenges when she returned to outdoor places like parklands, trail systems, and even national parks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Quinn Brett photographed in Chasm Meadows in Rocky Mountain National Park, Colorado (Photo: Courtesy of Brian Watson/Jacob Bailey).

Recent findings suggest that in 2017, National Park Service (NPS) climbing ranger Quinn Brett, 36, fell while ascending El Capitan in Yosemite National Park. The 120-foot drop left her paralyzed from the waist down. In a moment, she went from climbing the world’s steepest rock faces to moving in a wheelchair.

Like many Americans with mobility disabilities, Brett faced challenges when she returned to outdoor places like parklands, trail systems, and even national parks. Some of America’s wildest places were no longer accessible to her.

“To become disabled, and realize that I can’t even get across the street because there is a curb, for instance, was quite a change in perspective,” she told Climbing‘s sibling publication Outside.

That’s why Brett founded the accessibility consulting firm Dovetail Trail Consulting to make outdoor spaces more accessible and usable for everyone. With her help, the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) rolled out a latest interactive accessibility map on October 13, connecting visitors with trails, bathrooms, and campsites that are accessible to people with mobility disabilities.

“People with disabilities don’t want to just go to the one-mile paved trail in the busiest parts of our national parks,” Brett mentioned.

As part of the BLM map, visitors can snap photos of public lands and submit them, along with detailed descriptions of the infrastructure. Other users can then better understand accessibility before they hit the trail.

According to recent reports, “You don’t have to do a construction project,” Brett noted. “Just take pictures.”.

Nearly one in 10 Americans have mobility issues, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. For these people, Brett states enjoying the outdoors is not just about finding the right device, but also finding trails that are made for wheels.

“For a long time we only had one pair of shoes to pick, but now with mobility device technology, we have a whole bunch of types of shoes that we get to choose from, and we want to go use our shoes in a variety of places,” Brett said.

According to recent reports, kevin Oliver, chief of the BLM Division for Recreation and Business Services, participated in the three-year map project. He told Outside that the goal is to help people plan their trip and avoid surprises from site conditions.

Recent findings suggest that “We’re going to continue to work to deliver more information and better information to the recreation public, so that all types of interests can be served,” Oliver told Outside. “The BLM recognizes the work is never really done. You know, we’re always perfecting it.”.

The map includes 150 existing accessible recreation opportunities. One such example is McCoy Flats in Utah, a map entry that indicates the parking lot’s packed gravel, extended picnic tables, and the entrances to vault toilets.

The tool also identifies 74 additional sites where the BLM has proposed improvements. Some, like Colorado’s Blue Valley Ranch Trail, are fully funded and in progress. Others, such as Latest Mexico’s Glade Run Adaptive Trail, are still hunting for funding.

BLM’s latest map is one piece of a broader push to expand trail access across federal agencies.

It has been revealed that gathering the information is only the beginning. Julia Ray, chief operating officer of the adaptability nonprofit Move United, told Outside that keeping information up to date matters just as much.

“Trails are kind of living things,” Ray said. “They change with weather and seasons, so it has to be an ongoing process to keep that information current, and where and how that information is shared is still inconsistent.”.

Sources indicate that move United partnered with Mount Rainier and Grand Canyon National Parks to assess more than 17 miles of trails for accessibility. The organization also created a free trail-access course to help local land managers understand federal accessibility standards.

Improving access at popular trails is a great way to let more people share in the national park experience, Ray said.

Sources indicate that “If the public go to a trail more than others, that’s probably where anybody else would want to go as well,” she stated. “Everybody deserves the right to access the outdoors, and we are just really excited that there’s some energy around this right now.”.

Recent findings suggest that for trail consumers like Brett, having accessibility details means she can spend less time guessing and more time choosing where to go, what equipment to bring, and how much challenge she wants to take on. Her desire to be in the mountains hasn’t gone away, and as she says, it never will.

Recent findings suggest that “I still want to be playing and going to the top of mountains and doing wild and crazy things,” Brett says. “But I also need the information to decide what experience I want.”.

She added that including people with disabilities in trail assessment and information gathering can help land managers identify barriers. Some mobility devices can navigate rocks, roots, and steps; a narrow bridge or gate might stop someone instead.

Sources indicate that “Five miles of the trail might work totally fine, and then there’s a bridge to cross some water, and they just threw down a 12-inch bridge, and after that, there’s five more miles of trail that work just fine,” Brett remarked. “But if you’ve never hung out with somebody with a disability, then you might not know what is truly a barrier.”.

#205232. Remembering Chris Falkenstein, Long-time Yosemite Climber and Photographer

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (942 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Climbing ↗ Open Full Page

Remembering Chris Falkenstein, Long-time Yosemite Climber and Photographer

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (942 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Chris Falkenstein (left) and Don Reid (right) were long-time climbing partners and guidebook co-authors.
  • Chris Falkenstein passed away peacefully on August 9, 2026 after a brave and exhaustive battle with cancer.
  • It has been revealed that I grew up climbing with my Dad, but it was always his sport.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Chris Falkenstein (left) and Don Reid (right) were long-time climbing partners and guidebook co-authors. (Photo: Courtesy Falkenstein Family Collection).

Chris Falkenstein passed away peacefully on August 9, 2026 after a brave and exhaustive battle with cancer. Better known by many as Falky, Finkelstein, Steiny, Schwackenstein, or Commando, Chris wore many hats throughout his life: devoted husband and father, loyal friend, accomplished climber, photographer, skier, whitewater kayaker, windsurfer, mountain biker, self-proclaimed computer nerd, and passionate lover of Yosemite and the outdoors.

It has been revealed that I grew up climbing with my Dad, but it was always his sport. I enjoyed it, but pursued other sports. In a way, I don’t think I’ve found a climbing partner that was ever as dialed as he was. My Dad was so quiet and humble about his achievements; there were so many things he never mentioned. I remember being out climbing with him, when he would tell some story like, “We were out here in the ‘80s, blasting a boom box and climbing.” It turns out, he would be talking about a first ascent.

Those who knew him will remember his adventurous spirit, his enthusiasm for life, and the joy he found in exploring the world around him. His love for the outdoors was infectious. And the memories he created along the way will live on in those fortunate enough to have shared in his adventures.

Sources indicate that when Chris arrived in Yosemite in 1972, he brought a foundation of climbing experience from the Gunks of Upcoming York. His natural athleticism, determination, and enthusiasm swiftly drew him into the dynamic and evolving climbing scene of Yosemite Valley. What began as an introduction to the Yosemite climbing community grew into a lifelong passion and a lasting legacy.

In a recent development, he once remarked, “So off I went at 18 to explore climbing in Yosemite. Best decision of my life, and a true highlight… I consider my life beginning after 18. Stay young at heart forever if you can.”.

It has been revealed that chris spent the remainder of his life in and around Yosemite, calling many places home over the years, including Camp 4, the Annex, Badger Pass, Sonora, Tuolumne Meadows, and El Portal. Eventually, he settled in Foresta, where he and his wife, Doe, retired to the home they built together.

Recent findings suggest that throughout his years in Yosemite, Chris became a respected presence in the climbing community, known for being a quiet and humble force. He established multiple first ascents in Yosemite Valley and Tuolumne Meadows. Among his notable first ascents were Do or Fly (5.11c), The Speed of Life (5.11b), Black Angel (5.11a), and Highway Star (5.10a). Along with Don Reid, he co-authored Rock Climbs of Tuolumne Meadows, first published in 1983. Four additional editions later followed. He also authored Yosemite Sport Climbs in 1992. Through his climbs, guidebooks, and contributions to the community, Chris helped shape and document Yosemite’s rich climbing history.

Industry observers note that beyond his physical accomplishments in climbing, he inspired others and expanded the appreciation for the outdoors through his photography, videography, and online content. He captured the many aspects of climbing, mountaineering, and skiing, while sharing the extraordinary beauty of Yosemite.

Chris’s work appeared in a wide range of publications, climbing guides, gear catalogs, climbing films, commercials, Hollywood productions, and websites. Chris’s photography became a familiar part of the Yosemite landscape itself. As Don Reid once remarked with a teasing smirk, “You know you are made with Yosemite photography when your photos appear on the Coke machines, shuttle buses, and climbing guide covers of the place.”.

Recent findings suggest that when it was too cold to climb, Chris also had a deep love for winter sports. He played hockey throughout his life and contributed to the local pick up hockey club in Yosemite. Alongside Bruce Brossman and Loyd Price, Chris completed the first single-day trans-Sierra ski trip via Tioga Pass. His name also lives on through several first descents in the Sierras, including the Solstice Couloir and Powerhouse Chute.

Sources indicate that at Badger Pass Ski Resort, Chris spent many years serving as ski patrol manager. He brought his knowledge of climbing techniques into ski patrol training, developing methods for chairlift rescues and assisting with backcountry rescue efforts. His impact was perhaps best captured by a skier he helped, who later described him as “an angel emerging from the woods.”.

Early in his career, Chris worked for the Yosemite Climbing School, teaching climbing during the summer months and cross-country skiing in winter. He enjoyed summers as the employee housing manager in Tuolumne Meadows. In retirement, Chris continued to explore and enjoy the Sierras, while taking great pride in perfecting the art of being a grandfather. Chris also became an unofficial voice of Yosemite locals, keeping friends and former park residents connected to the place they loved by sharing updates and insights into the ever-changing landscape of Yosemite.

Chris loved everything Yosemite. He devoted much of his time to documenting not only the climbing, skiing, and athletic pursuits that made the park famous, but also its immense beauty, extensive history, and the development and change over time. With an eye for the extraordinary as well as the everyday, he captured the moments, places, and details that might otherwise go unnoticed. Through his lens and storytelling, Chris shared his deep appreciation for Yosemite. In so doing, he preserved a piece of its story for others.

Chris is survived by his wife Doe, his son Alex, his daughter-in-law Danielle, and his two-and-a-half-year-old grandson Finn, who loves trying to climb up anything in his path.

Latest Update: A Very Serious Story About Falling Asleep While Belaying

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1133 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The East Face of Mount Temple, Canada, and the scene of this story's shenanigans.
  • Substantial falls are commonplace while sport climbing and bouldering, but, in my opinion, the high alpine remains largely a safe space to take your brake hand off the rope.
  • According to recent reports, this old school state of mind deeply resonated with me earlier this month on a difficult alpine climb on Mount Temple in the Canadian Rockies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The East Face of Mount Temple, Canada, and the scene of this story's shenanigans. (Photo: Mitra Samavaki / Getty).

Substantial falls are commonplace while sport climbing and bouldering, but, in my opinion, the high alpine remains largely a safe space to take your brake hand off the rope. Why? With loose rock, aerated ice, and an often minimalist rack, falling off—even with a tight belay—usually spells disaster. A climber has every reason to follow the old “the leader cannot fall” ethos.

According to recent reports, this old school state of mind deeply resonated with me earlier this month on a difficult alpine climb on Mount Temple in the Canadian Rockies. This 1,400-meter ice and mixed route began easily enough, with a hike up a hard-packed snow slope at 6 a.m. toward the deep cleft that marked the start. Neither my partner Rory nor I were burdened with rope management during the first hour of climbing, since our rope stayed neatly coiled in a pack.

Hundreds of meters higher, below one of the crux pitches, we flaked out our rope. Above us stood a terribly skinny pillar of ice no wider than my shoulders at its base. Blue light filtered through its entirety, a sign of its youth and untrustworthiness.

“I don’t think I should place a screw in that,” Rory decided.

Industry observers note that I scanned the shattered quartzite behind the pillar, hoping to at least keep us attached to the mountain before Rory essentially soloed the pitch. Two nervous pitons and a shallow micro nut were all I could cobble together after 10 minutes of searching. I stomped out a waist-deep hole in the snow on the back side of the pillar and clipped into our wobbly anchor. My now four-piece anchor—plus Rory’s unshakeable climbing ability—gave us great odds of surviving his lead.

The runout pitch gave me ample opportunity to pay out slack as I pleased while munching on trail mix and rehydrating from our busy morning. After all, Rory was not allowed to fall, so he didn’t.

Falling has been a frowned-upon practice for most of climbing’s history, especially before sport climbing became popular in the 1980s. Only relatively recently, and only in some styles of climbing, have leader falls become no longer taboo—even acceptable and encouraged.

In a recent development, the crusty old-timer in me knows that, in any form of free climbing, it is always safer to climb to the top of a pitch without testing your equipment, be it a skinny rope, crashpad, or ice screw. This gut instinct evolved from a time when climbing gear was not completely trustworthy. Maybe you hand-stitched your quickdraw’s webbing yourself. Maybe you’d sourced your climbing protection from a hardware store. Or maybe you had tied your lead line around your waist because drop-seat harnesses hadn’t been invented yet. In this era—really only a few decades ago—your climbing ability was the first line of defense. Ropes and harnesses and removable protection served merely as dubious back-ups.

But the advent of regular whippers is a tragedy for one more reason: With newfangled belay devices, hang dogging, and constant pleas to “watch me,” belaying has become a real pain in the ass.

It has been revealed that nearly 12 hours later, Rory and I were still on Mount Temple. We’d topped out the ice climbing portion of the face and traversed across open snow slopes and through rock bands to a final serrated crux: the Black Towers. Countless turrets of dark limestone slice across the summit ridge of Mount Temple, creating difficult route finding even on a clear summer’s day. We were approaching midnight in November and a thick fog had choked the upper mountain. Visibility hovered around 10 meters. I had no idea where we were supposed to go.

It has been revealed that thankfully it was Rory’s lead again, and he was questing. Fifteen minutes ticked by as he wandered up a steep rocky groove, then another 15 of the rope unmoving. An hour passed. I clicked off my headlamp to save battery. More time passed. I figured I could tie off the rope and catch a few Zs, so I did. Sleep felt amazing. I was glad that even as we approached 24 hours on the move, Rory still knew the rules: The leader cannot fall. And the belayer gets to sleep.

I woke up to the sound of Rory’s voice. He’d been blocked by an overhang and was downclimbing. Thick, icy fog obscured our vision as I took the rack and traversed along a snow ledge looking for easier passage. The fog would sometimes lift for an instant—I’d spot a lonely star above—and I’d frantically flick my headlamp to full strength to catch a glimpse of the mountain. But before my eyes could adjust to the upcoming sight, the fog would crash back in like a breaking wave, drowning us in uncertainty once again.

In a recent development, this story does not end in a climbing success. We did not ultimately find our way through the Black Towers, nor did we share a weary, satisfied hug on the summit of Mount Temple. We became lost and a little delirious on a large mountain in the middle of the night and needed to go down.

We stayed roped together as we retraced our steps through deep snow on the upper mountain. I was a little worried about triggering an avalanche, but mainly I was just exhausted. If I stumbled, I would prefer to slide 30 meters before being caught by the rope than well over a thousand into the next life.

Recent findings suggest that rory and I regrouped at an anchor I’d built in an outcrop of yellow rock. He led out across another snowfield which terminated at a gigantic notch in an otherwise sheer ridgeline. The notch marked the start of a classic ski descent, the 60-degree Aemmer Couloir, and our escape hatch. Rory trudged toward it and I paid out rope, nodding off again.

Suddenly, I was awake. I had not pooped all day, yet the kilogram of trail mix and sausage and cheese I’d downed was making a basement appearance.

“Rory! Do you need a real belay for this bit? I really need to poo,” I yelled into the fog.

“No, I don’t care,” the fog yelled back.

I let the rope feed through the anchor, then unclipped it from my belay device and, without moving even a step away from our anchor, unloaded into the snow bank.

Industry observers note that it would have been a disgusting mess had Rory fallen and weighted the anchor, dragging me into my own steaming waste. But he didn’t, and I made it back to civilization with both my dignity and my life intact.

The Gozney Arc XL pizza oven makes outdoor entertaining easy year-round, from backyard pizza parties to après-ski gatherings. (Photo: Courtesy of Gozney).

I wrote about my Gozney Arc XL pizza oven two summers ago, when it became the pie de resistance for using my backyard to get outside more (and for a suspicious number of new friends showing up at my house). More than a year later, I’m happy to report that the novelty hasn’t worn off. If anything, I love it more.

It has been revealed that one of my favorite ways to spend a Sunday afternoon, or unwind after a mountain bike ride, is inviting friends over for homemade pizzas. Everyone brings their favorite toppings, we experiment with different combinations, and dinner becomes an activity in itself. It’s dinner and a show, and everyone gets fed. And because we keep ours on a covered porch with adequate ventilation, pizza night doesn’t end when winter arrives. Après-ski pizza parties might actually be my favorite use for it.

In a recent development, the Gozney Arc XL makes it ridiculously easy. It runs on propane (I use the same tank from my grill), reaches temperatures up to 950°F, and can cook a 16-inch pizza in as little as 60 seconds. Its lateral rolling flame distributes heat across the oven, so you don’t have to constantly rotate your pizza. The result is that perfectly blistered, chewy crust I usually associate with my favorite wood-fired pizza joints now in my own backyard.

Industry observers note that gozney makes several ovens, from more portable models to larger, more elaborate setups (many are also on sale right now). The Arc XL hits the sweet spot for me because it’s compact enough for our back patio, still with plenty of room to maneuver a full-size pizza.

Sources indicate that you can make your own dough, buy Gozney’s mixes, or do what we do: keep Trader Joe’s premade pizza dough in the freezer so we’re always ready for an impromptu pizza night. One tip: a little semolina flour on your pizza peel helps the dough slide into the oven without sticking.

Industry observers note that my favorite toppings? Peaches, burrata, prosciutto, basil, and hot honey. Comment yours!

Sources indicate that learn from my mistake. When I first bought my Arc XL, I skipped the matching stand for a cheaper rolling cart from Amazon. It was a nightmare to assemble, felt flimsy, and looked terrible. I recently upgraded to the actual Gozney stand, and the difference is night and day. It’s sturdy, streamlined, easy to move, and designed to hold the oven securely. I should have trusted Gozney from the start.

In a recent development, the stand has a 4.8-out-of-5-star rating from 204 customer reviews, so apparently plenty of people knew something I didn’t. Worth the upgrade, especially while it’s on sale.

If you’re shopping for someone who already owns a Gozney, the brand’s pizza peels, dough trays, and other accessories make excellent gifts and are also on sale for Black Friday.

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

In a recent development, overlanding is a pretty niche activity, so it can be hard to find the perfect gift for the driver in your life. Fear not. As an overlander myself, I’ve compiled a comprehensive gift list that has suggestions for overland rookies and veterans alike. I’ve included a wide range of price options, with some gift ideas so big they’ll take up half your living room and others small enough to fit under the tree.

Tires are the most vital overland upgrade. A good set of all-terrain tires like the BFGoodrich KO3s helps drivers safely get through snow and mud, and up and down rocky backcountry roads. Their tougher construction also helps resist flats. I love the KO3s for their legendary off-road reliability combined with their quiet ride on pavement.

Industry observers note that overlanders love to get stuck so they can get back out, which makes recovery gear essential. Maxtrax boards slip under tires that have lost traction, allowing the vehicle to slowly inch out of snow, mud, sand, or whatever else it’s bogged down in. Go for the more expensive Xtreme version because it comes with metal traction teeth that last significantly longer.

Industry observers note that airing down tires is often the easiest way to get unstuck because it increases the tires’ contact patch. I love the Rhino kit because it airs down four tires at once. I also recommend this ARB air compressor that attaches to a car battery and can reinflate the tires before you hit pavement again.

Sometimes self-recovery isn’t an option after getting stuck, and I’ve had to get yanked out by a friend. This device fits in the two-inch rear receiver on any truck or SUV and creates a safe place to attach a D-ring and recovery strap. Heads up: Make sure whoever you gift this to knows how to use it properly before heading out.

According to recent reports, folded down, this shovel is only 18 inches long. Fully extended, it goes to 34 inches and is perfect for digging your truck out of a snowbank or excavating a cathole near camp. I’ve tested an earlier version of this shovel for years, and the carbon steel head has put up with rocks, trees, and firm ground without ever bending or chipping.

Anyone who’s overlanding for more than a couple of days will love an electric fridge. It eliminates ice runs and keeps food from drowning in meltwater. Dometic makes some of the most reliable fridges on the market. I like this one because it has two zones: one a fridge, the other either a fridge or a freezer.

Coffee tastes better at 9,000 feet. To brew it there, Yeti’s indestructible French press is my go-to. I’ve thrown it in a kitchen box or just let it roll around in the back of my truck, and it still works perfectly every time. I also love that it has a ceramic lining so the coffee doesn’t taste like metal.

Water can be a precious commodity on a backcountry trip. That’s why I use this battery-powered faucet that pulls water from a jug and then dispenses just the right amount so I can wash my hands or do dishes. One charge lasts for weeks, and all the hoses are easy to clean at home. Pair it with a Dometic water jug for the ideal setup.

The REDARC GoBlock is my go-to overland battery (for fridges, lights, etc.) because it’s designed to be charged in multiple ways. I can connect solar panels to add juice at camp, or I can wire it to my alternator so it gets topped off while I’m driving. I recommend the kit version, which includes a dock that bolts to a truck bed and gives the battery a secure place to live at all times.

iKamper nailed the details with this version of the Skycamp rooftop tent. It has the smartest mounting system I’ve tested. The bombproof hardshell cover will put up with years of sun and weather, and inside it’s extra roomy thanks to a clever tent design. It’s pricey, but this is one of those buy-once, cry-once purchases that you’ll have for at least a decade.

Recent findings suggest that two layers of enhanced memory foam make the Foamy the most comfortable camping mat on the market. Nothing else I’ve tested even comes close. Perfect for larger tents or truck beds, the Foamy almost guarantees a good night’s sleep because it’s so plush. Pair it with a camping blanket and the setup will be almost as comfortable as what you’re used to at home.

Industry observers note that overlanding requires a lot of gear. The best way to keep it all organized is a Kitworks Gear Box. Infinitely customizable, the Gear Box is the perfect storage method for a camp kitchen, recovery gear, dry food, even clothing. Made from honeycomb panels covered in a 900-denier ripstop shell, the box has proven just as durable as any hard-sided competitor.

According to recent reports, don’t invest in a dash-mounted radio—get two of these instead. With an ultra-reliable, multi-day battery and huge range, these radios are the best way to stay in touch with buddies when cell phones don’t work. When I’m not using the radios in my truck, I use them to keep in contact while backcountry skiing, hunting, and other off-grid adventures.

Smoke rises from the Dragon Bravo Fire on the Grand Canyon’s North Rim in July 2025. The wildfire burned more than 145,000 acres and destroyed 114 structures, including the historic Grand Canyon Lodge (Photo: slovegrove/Getty).

On November 23, Grand Canyon National Park Superintendent Ed Keable confirmed his initiative to retire at the end of 2026, after more than six years overseeing the park.

“As Geoffrey Chaucer wrote, ‘All good things must come to an end.’ So, too, my time at GRCA,” Keable wrote in a November 23 email to park employees obtained by Arizona Public Radio station KNAU. In the email, he confirmed that his last day will be December 31 and that agency leaders are working to identify an acting superintendent to take over on January 1.

Keable’s announcement came just ten days after the Department of the Interior released a damning 65-page investigative report detailing how leadership failures, inadequate preparation, and communication breakdowns contributed to the devastating 2025 Dragon Bravo Fire, which destroyed 114 structures on the park’s North Rim, including the historic Grand Canyon Lodge.

The investigation drew on interviews with more than 70 people and a review of over 18,000 documents, including fire management looks and communication logs.

Keable’s retirement email made no mention of the Dragon Bravo Fire or the Interior Department’s investigative report.

“I have made this decision for very personal reasons,” Keable wrote.

Outside contacted Keable and the National Park Service for comment but did not receive a response as of the publishing of this story.

According to recent reports, A career government attorney, Keable spent 23 years in the Interior Department’s Office of the Solicitor, including eight years as assistant solicitor of general law, before his appointment in April 2020 during President Donald Trump’s first administration. He had no previous experience working for the National Park Service.

The Coalition to Protect America’s National Parks, an organization representing current and former park service employees, issued a statement on April 3, 2020, criticizing Keable’s selection the same day the NPS revealed his appointment.

“Ed Keable is not qualified to manage and lead a complicated park such as the Grand Canyon,” Phil Francis, then-chair of the coalition, remarked in the statement.

In the appointment announcement, NPS Deputy Director David Vela praised Keable’s leadership abilities and cited his experience within the Interior Department as an asset to the park.

Sparked by lightning on July 4, 2025, the Dragon Bravo Fire burned more than 145,000 acres over nearly three months and cost an estimated $141 million to suppress, according to the federal report. Investigators concluded that “the most consequential drivers were not environmental,” finding that many of the challenges the NPS and firefighters encountered during the blaze were “foreseeable, preventable, and reflective of broader institutional issues.”.

In the report, investigators determined that “leadership roles did not align with expertise or decision making authority.” As the fire’s agency administrator, Keable was responsible for overseeing firefighting strategy and authorizing suppression tactics.

Under NPS guidelines, superintendents at wildfire-prone parks are expected to qualify for that role within two years of their appointment. Five years into his tenure, Keable still lacked that qualification, the report remarked. Although qualified administrators were available locally, the park didn’t bring one in until July 30, nearly four weeks after the fire ignited.

According to recent reports, keable initially approved a strategy known as confine and contain, which involves keeping a wildfire within designated boundaries rather than extinguishing it entirely. The approach conflicted with 2025 federal guidance against managing wildfires for ecological benefit, though investigators indicated that Keable had not received that, the report said.

Park leadership reaffirmed the strategy twice over the next five days, during which the fire breached planned containment lines.

“Continued authorization of the confine and contain strategy did not reflect awareness of changing conditions or escalating risk,” investigators wrote.

According to recent reports, communication failures also delayed firefighters’ efforts to slow the blaze using aerial fire retardant. Keable authorized retardant drops on July 13, once an earlier request from firefighters was clarified, but by then, the Grand Canyon Lodge had already burned.

The report stopped short of assigning individual fault. “The Dragon Bravo Fire should be understood as a warning event,” the report stated. “The findings demonstrate outcomes were shaped less by tactical execution than by NPS systemic issues related to authority, qualifications, and decision processes.”.

As Outside reported in April, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum suggested that full suppression might have prevented hundreds of millions of dollars in property losses, though wildland firefighters noted that the canyon’s steep terrain initially made ground operations unsafe.

Industry observers note that the National Park Service advertised Keable’s position on November 24, with applications closing December 8 and an annual salary ranging from $162,740 to $228,000. Responsibilities include overseeing wildland firefighting, emergency medical services, and backcountry rescues.

The job hunt comes at a pressing time for the national park. A devastating flash flood on August 29 destroyed trails and infrastructure along the Colorado River and led to three deaths. Facilities on the South Rim went without running water for nearly two months until the park restored water service to six lodges on November 20.

According to recent reports, among the next superintendent’s biggest challenges will be rebuilding the North Rim. Earlier this month, the park service concluded a public comment period on three preliminary redevelopment concepts for the area. Congress is also considering the North Rim Restoration Act, which would give the park service greater contracting flexibility to expedite reconstruction.

Sections of the fire-damaged North Rim reopened to visitors in May, but the August flash flood hindered reconstruction efforts, washing out trails and damaging bridges and critical infrastructure. The entire North Kaibab Trail and Cottonwood Campground remain closed, and Phantom Ranch’s lodging closure has been extended through January 31, 2027.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Within a few hours, Dakota Jackson, senior director of visitor engagement at the Appalachian Trail Conservancy (ATC) had written back to set up a meeting.
  • Industry observers note that from her Philadelphia studio, Weston had a sense of what a good walk could yield.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, when Philadelphia metalsmith Mallory “Bullseye” Weston wanted to apply for an artist residency on the Appalachian Trail, she ran into a problem. They didn’t have one.

So she sent a cold email. Within a few hours, Dakota Jackson, senior director of visitor engagement at the Appalachian Trail Conservancy (ATC) had written back to set up a meeting. It was perfect timing: The ATC was approaching its centennial in 2025 and looking for newly introduced ways to get more hikers on trail. As Caroline Ralston, the ATC’s associate vice president of marketing and communications, put it, “at that time, we realized we didn’t really have anything for creatives.”.

Industry observers note that from her Philadelphia studio, Weston had a sense of what a good walk could yield. She’d already put in miles on the John Muir Trail (JMT), the Pacific Crest Trail (PCT), and the Tahoe Rim Trail, and was starting to see a clearer connection between her creative life and her hiking.

A 454-mile stretch of the PCT found its way into 30 titanium brooches shaped like lengths of paracord. Their colors and patterns changed with her mood on the trail, day by day. Her stories became a zine. So when she and Jackson started talking through possible structures for the ATC’s inaugural artist in residence program, she offered herself up as the guinea pig.

In a recent development, last year, when the Conservancy officially launched the program, Weston set out from Georgia as its pilot creative. “Almost a year after I planted the seed for this wild idea, somehow, things came together to make it a reality,” Weston wrote in her blog.

Sources indicate that since metalwork is specialized and far from portable, she used the hike as an inspiration gathering exercise rather than a time to actually create work. She couldn’t haul a forge, but she could carry a camera. Back in Philadelphia, she’s been picking through her thousands of photographs, taking another look at the pile of butterfly wings she came across, or the blazes she passed.

“Hiking the trail as the ATC’s Artist in Residence has motivated me to be more observant of my surroundings,” Weston told the ATC. “I’ve been actively documenting the experience through photography and journaling, wanting to remember the rich details of my hike and use them to generate artwork from the vivid text and images I’ve collected.”.

Weston had one piece finished before she ever set foot on the AT. For the trail’s centennial, she designed an enamel pin that hikers could pick up at a visitor center.

The ATC is now looking for its 2027 Artist in Residence, and artists working in any medium have until January 3, 2027, to apply. The residency includes a limited stipend for transportation and lodging for events along the AT, and a two- to four-week stay at Maine’s Monson Arts, an arts center in the last town NOBO hikers pass through before the 100-Mile wilderness. Weston spent five months walking the entire AT, but the next resident could hike a section or spend their time in one town along the trail; the residency’s structure is malleable.

According to recent reports, “This program is a upcoming way to experience the trail,” indicates Ralston. “When the trail was first conceptualized over 100 years ago, one of the founding ideas was that people need a place to escape, connect with nature, and unplug. This program is an extension of that. We want to invite artists to immerse themselves on the trail, connect with nature, and see what kind of inspiration comes from it.”.

Along with a résumé or CV and five to 10 work samples, applicants must provide an artist statement and a work proposal. The ATC wants to know what you make, what time on the trail might bring to your work, and how you’d share it.

What makes an application stand out? For Ralston, notable applications will express “a desire to get out there, and a desire to share it publicly.” For Weston, that meant giving talks at trail centers.

Her advice to the next applicant? Think about what a stretch of time on this particular trail might change about the work you already do, and leave yourself some room to be surprised. For Weston, one of those surprises came in her first week out of Georgia.

According to recent reports, the first time Weston spotted pink lady’s slipper orchids on the AT, her husband was hiking with her. He’d come along for the first stretch and they saw a few patches together that week. Each flower had a little pouch that she found “kind of weird and grotesque looking, but also very beautiful.” By the time she came across a whole field of them, her husband had gone home to Philadelphia. “I’m all alone, and here’s all these orchids,” she remembers thinking.

Industry observers note that now, back in her Philadelphia studio, she’s working on a recreation of a pink lady’s slipper. Of all the things she saw in five months on trail, that one made what she calls a “one to one translation” into her work.

“Now that I’m back in Philadelphia, I’m distilling all of that experience into work that emerges from it,” notes Weston.

Better for the Sea, Better for You

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Canned seafood has long been a staple of the outdoor menu: It’s portable, nutritious, and adds a ton of flavor to simple meals.
  • In a recent development, thanks to pioneering efforts to establish sustainable fishing practices—and make them transparent for consumers—it’s easier than ever to find options that support our complex marine ecosystems.
  • According to the most recent data from the National Seafood Association, canned tuna is the third most popular seafood in the United States.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Canned seafood has long been a staple of the outdoor menu: It’s portable, nutritious, and adds a ton of flavor to simple meals. And it’s not just for hikers and campers. Canned and pouched seafood has been steadily rising in popularity in recent years, thanks in part to its protein, omega-3 fatty acids, and convenience. But while tuna can be a great choice for your health, how do you know if it’s a good choice for the environment?

In a recent development, thanks to pioneering efforts to establish sustainable fishing practices—and make them transparent for consumers—it’s easier than ever to find options that support our complex marine ecosystems. Here’s why it matters.

According to the most recent data from the National Seafood Association, canned tuna is the third most popular seafood in the United States. That means a lot of tuna harvested from the world’s oceans, making harmful fishing practices even more harmful due to the enormity of the scale. This puts tuna and other fish populations at risk, and unfortunately, these practices still dominate the industry.

Purse seine fishing, which is responsible for about 66% of global tropical tuna catch, per the International Seafood Sustainability Foundation, can be harmful, especially when used in conjunction with fish aggregating devices (FADs). This method involves using a large wall of netting—up to 6,500 feet long and reaching around 650 feet in depth—to surround an entire school of fish. Non-selective mass fishing practices can deplete a population before it has a chance to properly reproduce, especially since it indiscriminately removes juvenile tuna from the ecosystem, threatening healthy repopulation.

Another key threat from large-scale industrial fishing is bycatch, or the unintentional harvesting of non-targeted species. Some of the species most impacted by the tuna industry include sharks, sea turtles, and marine mammals like dolphins. Net-based fishing with FADs is the most common culprit, since FADs don’t discriminate between which types of fish they attract. Bycatch also frequently occurs with longline fishing, which uses baited lines an average of 28 miles long. Animals caught as bycatch often do not survive.

How can things be done differently? Wild Planet is a case study. Since 2004, Wild Planet has focused on sourcing seafood through responsible fishing practices. Its wild albacore and skipjack tuna showcase how responsible fishing and high-quality products can—and should—go hand in hand.

Sources indicate that all of Wild Planet’s tuna are caught individually using pole-and-line or trolling methods. Pole-and-line is exactly what it sounds like: one pole, one line, and one fish at a time. Trolling is similar, with multiple lines towed behind a slow-moving boat. Both the bait used and the speed at which the boat travels are specifically chosen to attract the targeted species. In both methods, fish are hauled in immediately, so non-targeted species can be promptly released.

Industry observers note that the benefits of these inherently selective methods are twofold. First, they allow Wild Planet to specifically target tuna while minimizing bycatch of other marine species. Additionally, the company’s responsible fishing operations are able to further select what kind of tuna is being harvested. Wild Planet sources younger migratory tuna near the ocean’s surface, avoiding juvenile fish, who are key to repopulation efforts, and older, larger tuna that tend to accumulate higher levels of mercury. It’s an approach that’s better for you and the planet.

In a recent development, the Monterey Bay Aquarium Seafood Watch Program has a name for foods like this: Super Greens. It’s an exclusive list—it right now includes only 10 foods—that points to pole-and-line caught tuna as an option that’s high in omega-3s, low in mercury, and harvested with the ocean in mind.

According to recent reports, the Monterey Bay Aquarium has a unique relationship with Wild Planet. The brand has not only been following the aquarium’s guidance since the beginning, but the institution is actually key to the firm’s origin story. It was at a Monterey Bay Aquarium exhibit on fragile ocean ecosystems that Wild Planet founder Bill Carvalho was inspired to build a different kind of seafood company.

According to recent reports, the Aquarium, in turn, is inspired by the efforts that many in the industry have taken in response to its suggestions. “Some of these companies have been with us from the very beginning,” Shawn Cronin, market engagement director for Seafood Watch mentioned in 2024. “They make it easy for people to choose responsible seafood day-to-day, helping move the needle through their sourcing and by directly engaging in global improvement initiatives. It’s not an easy commitment to make.”.

That emphasis on doing what’s right and trusting the science continues today. It’s the kind of thinking that guides the way Wild Planet fishes as well as the types of fish it sells. In addition to tuna, Wild Planet also sells mackerel, anchovies, and sardines. These smaller, lower-food-chain species can be more abundant and offer another responsibly sourced seafood option, while delivering plenty of protein, omega-3s, and flavor.

In a recent development, if you’re looking to incorporate more sustainable seafood into your life, the same principles extend beyond tuna. Always look for labels that call out pole-and-line caught, troll caught, and/or FAD-free fishing. Other information, like the specific species and where it was harvested, lets you know that the company knows—and cares—where its fish come from.

You can find out what sustainability tastes like for yourself. From now until December 22, Outside readers get 20% off everything on Wild Planet’s website with code OUTSIDE20. Because even though the impact of our choices might be harder to see when it’s an ocean away, it’s no less important.

In a recent development, founded in 2004, Wild Planet is the first large-scale sustainably focused canned seafood manufacturer in the U.S. Committed to protecting marine ecosystems for future generations, Wild Planet sources 100% wild-caught seafood using the highest sustainability standards, delivering nutrient-dense, minimally processed products that are as close to nature as possible. Learn more at WildPlanetFoods.com.

  • A hiker died on November 22 after reportedly slipping on ice and falling approximately 500 feet while trying to help his son on Mount Baden-Powell, a 9,399-foot peak in Southern California’s San Gabriel Mountains, according to a GoFundMe organized by the hiker’s niece.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Snow covers the slopes of Southern California's San Gabriel Mountains, where a hiker died on November 22 after reportedly slipping on ice and falling approximately 500 feet on Mount Baden-Powell (Photo: Noah Sauve/Getty Images).

A hiker died on November 22 after reportedly slipping on ice and falling approximately 500 feet while trying to help his son on Mount Baden-Powell, a 9,399-foot peak in Southern California’s San Gabriel Mountains, according to a GoFundMe organized by the hiker’s niece.

Recent findings suggest that the GoFundMe page identified the man as Guillermo Alejandro Batres. His niece, Jennifer Morse, wrote on the fundraising page that Batres and his son were attempting to summit the mountain when the younger man slipped and fell. When Batres tried to help him up, he lost his footing and fell down a steep gulch.

Recent findings suggest that “On this mountain, there’s no room for error if you slip when it’s snowy or icy out,” Cris Hazzard, a Southern California hiking expert who has climbed Baden-Powell dozens of times, told Outside. “If you slip in the summer, you probably just fall on your butt, maybe go down some gravel. You slip in the winter, you’re going down hundreds, if not thousands, of feet.”.

Recent findings suggest that AV Scanner News, a local outlet that monitors emergency dispatches, reported that authorities received a call about the incident around 10:09 A.M. after the hikers encountered snow and ice roughly three miles from the Vincent Gap trailhead. Los Angeles County firefighters and sheriff’s deputies responded near mile marker 71 on Angeles Crest Highway. Authorities also requested the sheriff’s department’s Air Rescue 5 helicopter crew to recover Batres’s body, according to the outlet.

Authorities have not independently confirmed the family’s account of the fall, and the sheriff’s department did not respond to Outside‘s request for comment before publication.

According to recent reports, located in Angeles National Forest northeast of Los Angeles, Baden-Powell is a popular warm-weather climb. The standard summit route begins at Vincent Gap, a 6,585-foot mountain pass along Angeles Crest Highway. From there, hikers follow the Pacific Crest Trail for roughly four miles, climbing more than 2,800 feet through 35 wooded switchbacks up the mountain’s north face before reaching an exposed ridge near the summit.

Because the mountain’s north-facing slopes receive less direct sunlight, snow tends to linger there, Hazzard told Outside. During warmer days, that snow can melt and refreeze overnight, leaving patches of ice along the trail. Although the San Gabriel Mountains receive snow every winter, the conditions can catch visitors off guard so close to Los Angeles.

Batres had hiked Baden-Powell at least once before, according to the GoFundMe, and Hazzard noted that even experienced hikers face heightened risk once ice forms on the route.

Industry observers note that “If you are experienced and you know the dangers, there’s still a higher risk of something going wrong than there would be without that snow or ice, regardless of how careful you are,” Hazzard said. “Each winter, we get people going up there who don’t really understand that the hike they did in the summer is now a mountaineering exercise. It’s so steep, and there are dangerous runouts. If you slip, you might hit your head. There’s a lot you can bang into on the way down.”.

Batres’s death occurred just two days after another hiker survived a serious fall on the same mountain. In a November 21 statement on X, the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department described rescuing a hiker who had slid more than 300 feet down a snowy chute on Baden-Powell on November 20.

Responders initially struggled to locate the person due to inaccurate GPS coordinates, completing the rescue shortly before worsening weather would have grounded the helicopter.

According to recent reports, similar falls have occurred in past winters. In February 2016, a 69-year-old hiker slid roughly 100 feet down an icy chute before a sheriff’s helicopter airlifted him to a trauma center. Nearby Mount Baldy has also experienced deadly winter accidents, including three hiking fatalities in the first week of January 2026.

Despite having climbed Baden-Powell in winter with experienced mountaineers using crampons, Hazzard remarked he now avoids the peak once snow arrives. Instead, he recommends seeking formal mountaineering training before attempting snow-covered summits or choosing lower-elevation desert trails around Joshua Tree and Palm Springs.

Industry observers note that “They shouldn’t do it in the winter,” Hazzard stated. “But winter is the great time to go and do the hikes you can’t safely do in summer, and leave the high peaks alone.”.

Since the dawn of time, the base layer/midlayer/shell sandwich has been the go-to for winter adventures. Today’s jackets use the latest advances in insulation and waterproofing to replace two or three traditional layers, and adapt better to changing conditions and activity levels.

According to recent reports, the jackets in this review proved sufficiently lightweight, breathable, and weatherproof that we rarely had to remove them to manage heat—and when we did, it was much easier to deal with one item than several. We tested these jackets in conditions ranging from wind-blown fall rain to frigid cold mountain mornings, and they consistently kept us moving forward with minimal fuss, wrapped in warmth and shielded from the elements.

Pros and Cons + Surprisingly warm + Unrestrictive fit + Smart vent panels – No hood.

The Thermalrunner proved an excellent choice for a surprisingly broad range of temperatures and weather conditions. On a blustery 40-degree day with light rain, the water-resistant fabric treatment handled the challenge, beading moisture on the exterior while the soft interior lining stayed dry against the skin. On another run when the sun burned through clouds unexpectedly fast, we were impressed by how well the vent panels in the back shed excess heat. One tester called the lightweight PrimalLoft insulation a “Goldilocks” amount of warmth that consistently tamed the chill without overheating him.

Industry observers note that this jacket features all the premium touches you’d want, including zip hand pockets and chest pouch, reflective patches, and a slightly extended, insulated back panel that added extra warmth and protection from the elements. Paired with a light, short-sleeved base layer, the Thermalrunner jacket was comfortable for running on mild 50-degree days, and with a hat (it lacks a hood), gloves, and a long-sleeve undergarment, it handled near-freezing weather just as well.

Pros and Cons + Featherweight + Packable + Protective hood – Fragile.

Recent findings suggest that stuffing the Aerolight Wind Jacket into a pack before heading out on an adventurous mountain trek in the Swiss Alps proved to be a good decision for one tester. Late in the afternoon, the summer skies filled with clouds, the temperature dropped, and bursts of rain started soaking the mountainside. The jacket provided immediate warmth, blocked the wind, and, though it’s by no means waterproof, kept enough moisture out to keep moving comfortably—with almost no weight penalty.

The water-resistant treatment is PFAS-free, and small touches like an adjustable hood and elastic wrist cuffs add to the better-than-expected protection. The ultralight fabric is soft and quiet on the move and breathes well at high exertion levels, but offers no stretch. The lone chest pocket doubles as a stuff sack, making this a great item to keep on hand for mild days in the 40s and 50s. The feather-weight construction comes at the price of being somewhat more fragile than other top picks: we’ve heard reports of the fabric blowing out under stress, although we didn’t see any excess wear during testing.

Pros and Cons + Windproof + Highly visible + Distinctive look – Lacks breathability.

When was the last time someone on the street complimented your running outfit for looking good? Our testers got compliments on the PYNRS (pronounced like “pioners”) Magnolia Track Jacket all the time. This NYC-based tech giant started as an inclusive urban running club before branching into apparel; the result is functional outerwear that stands out from the crowd.

The iridescent, tightly woven nylon shell features reflective piping for excellent visibility from all sides, and the polyester lining is soft against skin. Cut on the looser side, this jacket easily accommodated insulating layers and proved comfortable for running in near- and sub-freezing weather. It offers roomy, zippered hand pockets and an interior zippered chest pocket, plus elasticized cuffs and a drawstring waist to seal out the weather. The jacket is a little hefty and lacks some of the breathability higher-performance materials offer, but for cool-to-cold weather running (low 40s to mid-20s), we stayed comfortably warm and looked stylish in the Magnolia Track Jacket.

Recent findings suggest that start ready and stay ready with this do-anything hooded workout layer. Crafted from a soft performance stretch knit, this jacket is both insulating and flexible with a protective woven overlay that gives you added coverage in cool and variable conditions. It wicks moisture and includes a drawcord hood and zip pockets to keep you and your belongings dry and safe in any weather. Pair it with the Vuori Sunday bottoms to make the perfect set.

Pros and Cons + Soft wool fabric + Polartec insulation + Wind-blocking torso – No reflectivity.

The Alpha Active’s medium-weight blend of Merino wool and polyester, with a touch of bamboo rayon, proved exceptionally soft and warm, and excelled at wicking moisture away from skin. Baffled Polartec Alpha insulation and a wind-blocking nylon fabric overlay the chest. The overall effect felt like wearing a lightweight vest over a premium base-layer shirt—but integrated into a single piece that moved comfortably and quietly with us.

The breathable Merino-blend sleeves and back, with no wind-blocking material, kept us from overheating at easier paces up to the 50-degree mark. The jacket proved comfortable down to freezing when working hard—adding a lightweight outer shell produced a warm combination that handled all but the most bitter or windy conditions. The sleek fit and black fabric look good, but bring a reflective hat or wear a light for nighttime running.

Pros and Cons + Toasty, 95% recycled fleece front + Functional and stylish fit + Solid warmth – No backside windblock.

In a recent development, our testers agreed that the front of this attractive jacket provided solid insulation for frigid conditions. They were divided, however, on whether it would have benefited from better wind-blocking on the back, where a large fabric panel vented heat, leaving some feeling too exposed to the elements. Still, at an affordable price, most reviewers found the Winter Warm Pro kept them comfortable in temperatures well below freezing (there’s no hood, so bring a hat for frigid days). The body fabric fleece is made with 95 percent recycled materials, feels soft against bare skin, and stretches nicely. The polyester torso insulation is reassuringly thick without feeling bulky. Additional touches include a water-repellent coating, hand pockets, side mesh storage pocket, and a zippered chest pocket.

Pros and Cons + Stormproof + Effective hood and brim + Chest snap – Crinkly.

According to recent reports, salomon’s adv.DRY material—a thin, microporous membrane bonded to a nylon shell—proved impressively waterproof during drenching rain showers while staying breathable in dry conditions. The Bonatti Pro features fully taped seams, waterproof zippers, and an excellent, adjustable brimmed hood that kept our hair dry and our heads warm without impeding our field of vision, even on the move. A snap closure at the chest lets you open the zipper and vent heat rapidly without removing the jacket, and reflective patches on the front and back provide good visibility in poor weather.

In a recent development, the fit is close yet roomy enough to accommodate insulating underlayers, extending the jacket’s comfortable range below the freezing mark. The fabric is somewhat crinkly, but it still packs easily into a small bundle. There are vents at the waist, but they’re fairly minimal, and we didn’t notice much airflow. Salomon’s “aeroPACK” flap system is meant to accommodate a small hydration backpack without impeding the jacket’s fit; we didn’t test this feature but noted that it didn’t get in the way when running without a pack.

Choosing the best winter running jacket is primarily about the kinds of winter conditions you face where you live, travel, and run. Consider if you need a waterproof layer, or can get by with water resistance—waterproof jackets are more costly, don’t breathe as well, and tend to be somewhat stiffer and noisier, but are worth it when you’re out in a downpour or blizzard.

Then think about whether you want your running jacket to be insulated and provide warmth on its own, or work as a thin, exterior shell layer. Insulated jackets can make heading out in frigid temps less daunting, especially if you tend to run cold, but can get hot during high-intensity exercise or if the temps rise. Shell jackets allow you to layer underneath to adjust for a range of conditions. Also consider whether you want a fitted jacket that stays close to the body for streamlined mobility, or a looser fit that allows flexibility for layering underneath.

The jacket review test crew put these products through their paces in locations as diverse as the Swiss Alps and Nebraska’s High Plains, logging miles on both roads and trails. Testers recorded their notes for each sample piece during easy runs, up-tempo workouts, and everything in between, in good weather and full-on storm conditions. Jackets were evaluated for their effectiveness at keeping testers warm and blocking wind and moisture while breathing and venting excess heat, with bonus points given for the versatility to handle a range of weather conditions and to look good in diverse contexts.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A helicopter transports a deceased hiker recovered from Humboldt Peak. (Photo: Custer County Sheriff's Office).

A hiker who went missing on a Colorado 14er earlier this week was found dead from an apparent fall on November 24, following a three-day search that sent rescuers combing the high country in winter conditions.

Custer County Search and Rescue (CCSAR) remarked in a press release that a Colorado Army National Guard helicopter participating in the search spotted “evidence of a fatal fall.” Rescuers were able to confirm the deceased was the missing man, a 31-year-old from the Denver area who CCSAR described as an experienced hiker.

Authorities noted that the hiker had summited 14,068-foot Humboldt Peak solo early on the morning of Sunday, November 22. At 5 p.m., CCSAR was notified that the hiker still hadn’t returned, and sent teams into the field alongside aerial support from Reach Air and Flight for Life. The missing hiker had shared his strategy with his family; however, while rescuers rapidly located his car, they were unable to locate him despite searching through the night in winter weather. Additional ground teams joined the search the following morning, but fared no better.

According to recent reports, after pausing the search for the night, 21 volunteers, including K9 teams and drone operators, returned to the field on Tuesday. During the operation, authorities closed the South Colony area to cars and hikers.

In a statement, the Custer County Sheriff’s Office offered its condolences to the deceased hiker’s family, friends, and fiancé, and noted that both the hiker’s plan and cell phone forensics helped authorities determine where they should look.

It has been revealed that compared to other 14ers in the same area, the hike up Humboldt is relatively straightforward. The standard West Ridge route follows the feature of the same name roughly 11 miles out and back to the summit. During fall and winter, however, snow and ice can both make it more difficult to stay on-route and increase the consequences of a slip on the peak’s exposed ridgeline. It was not immediately clear which route the hiker took to the summit.

The nearby South Colony SNOTEL station, which sits at 10,800 feet, recorded 16 inches of snow on the ground on November 22, up nearly 7 inches from the week prior.

The Tour du Mont Blanc Is Getting New Rules in 2027. Having a Guide Is More Important Than Ever.

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1715 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outsideonline

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A view of the of the Alps on Tour du Mont Blanc.
  • Industry observers note that the trail ahead of us narrows to a ledge, with rock on our left and a sheer drop on our right, camouflaged by trees.
  • Moments like that are becoming more common with more trekkers on the Tour du Mont Blanc (TMB), the 170-kilometer (106-mile) loop around Western Europe’s highest peak through France, Italy, and Switzerland.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A view of the of the Alps on Tour du Mont Blanc. (Photo: Getty).

Industry observers note that the trail ahead of us narrows to a ledge, with rock on our left and a sheer drop on our right, camouflaged by trees. After hearing the now-familiar heavy breaths of runners behind me, I move to the mountainside to let them pass. It’s mid-August, and the Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc (UTMB), the ultramarathon circling Mont Blanc, is kicking off later this month in Chamonix. We started our own Tour du Mont Blanc in Chamonix, the mountain town known as the birthplace of alpinism, which was buzzing with excitement and packs of runners strapped into hydration packs. Ahead of me, a young man is stopped on the narrow dirt trail, calling out to a friend on the forest slope below. Before I can even turn around, our guide, Jason Day, springs into action, grabs a rope from his pack, and helps pull the hiker, whose pack had tumbled down the slope, back to safety.

Moments like that are becoming more common with more trekkers on the Tour du Mont Blanc (TMB), the 170-kilometer (106-mile) loop around Western Europe’s highest peak through France, Italy, and Switzerland. Roughly 80,000 people hike it each year, and visits are up about 50 percent since 2020. “People can only see the backsides of those in front of them,” Jean-Marc Peillex, mayor of Saint-Gervais-les-Bains, a mountain town at the base of Mont Blanc in France, told Swiss broadcaster SRF. That wasn’t my exact experience for most of the trek, but in a few places, especially near Chamonix, the trail was congested.

According to recent reports, chamonix and the six other French towns along the TMB route, from Vallorcine to Bourg-Saint-Maurice and Beaufort, have drafted a charter to manage crowds, with local officials aiming to put it in place by spring 2027, ahead of next year’s trekking season. The upcoming rules, aiming to curb overtourism and help slow environmental damage, are awaiting final signature. The key proposals include reservations for every night on the trail; a ban on wild camping, with paid, bookable bivouac areas replacing the informal spots; and new limits on luggage transfers. Guided groups would be capped at twelve and led by guides trained in rescue and licensed in all three countries.

Industry observers note that the charter is voluntary, covers only France for now, and still depends on local ordinances for enforcement. But the message is clear: the era of showing up and figuring it out on the TMB is ending. Chamonix’s mayor, François-Xavier Laffin, who is similarly introducing quotas at nearby Lac Blanc, an alpine lake also suffering from its popularity, puts it this way: “To reserve is to preserve.”.

In a recent development, adding to the growing traffic on the trail are the effects of climate change on the Alps. Rising summer temperatures are accelerating permafrost thaw and glacier retreat, contributing to record rockfall activity in the Mont Blanc massif. While this mostly impacts the summit climbing routes, hot summers also change trail and water conditions for hikers on the Tour du Mont Blanc.

“As for the environmental impacts, trail erosion is of course the most obvious one, but we must also take into account wild bivouacking, which has multiplied, with impacts on the flora as well as the disturbance of wildlife,” states Daniel Rodrigues, general director of the Compagnie des Guides de Chamonix, the oldest mountain guide organization in the world.

It has been revealed that “The reservation system is fair. Everyone can book their places, and tour operators can do the same. So the same rules apply to everyone, including amateur mountain users, and that matters to us: the mountains are a space of freedom,” says Rodrigues. “That remarked, this space must be protected, in terms of biodiversity and environmental impacts, but also economically.”.

The charter puts licensed mountain professionals at the center of safety on the trail. According to Rodrigues, that means operators will no longer be able to sell self-guided packages (just bookings and transfers) and will have to include a guide certified in all three countries.

“This is a major step forward, because the guide ensures that everyone stays safe and that everything goes smoothly. It also creates work for local people and delivers a genuine positive impact on the inhabitants of this mountain range,” adds Rodrigues.

Recent findings suggest that I hiked the Tour du Mont Blanc in August with Live Breathe Hike, and I came home convinced that, especially under the potential new rules, having a local guide is no longer a luxury. It’s the smartest way to hike this trail.

According to recent reports, the TMB isn’t one trail; rather, there are a lot of different paths and detours.”There’s a classic route, but there’s a lot of different variants,” says Allison Fleece, cofounder of WHOA Travel, a women’s adventure-travel company that runs guided trips, including on the Tour du Mont Blanc. Some variants are higher and more exposed; others go along lower valleys. On our third day, instead of following the crowds, Day led us off the Col du Bonhomme on a variant toward Lac de Roselend, where we barely saw another hiker for miles. “You feel like you have the place to yourself,” says Live Breathe Hike founder Tanya Perret, who started the Chamonix-based trekking company in 2016 and says she has guided the TMB more than 75 times.

Industry observers note that under the proposed rules, every night would have to be booked in advance, across three countries with different systems. Guides already do that work, and finding gems to stay at like Le Chalet de Roselend takes deep knowledge of the area. With only ten rooms, the chalet, whose balconies overlook the Lac de Roselend, was a godsend after one of our longest days of trekking. Years ago, Perret drove there to book it in person, because the elderly owner at the time only took reservations face to face. The young couple who now runs it cooks traditional dishes with local produce.

According to recent reports, the charter asks operators to buy local and partner with local producers. Good guides already do. “Many of the places that we stay are generational families, and I’ve known those families for 30 years,” claims Perret. On our trip, that meant a stop at a family cheese farm as well as the small lakeside chalet. “That’s the micro-economy,” adds Perret.

Nearly every day on my trek, Day chose a variant. Perret says the choice comes down to two factors: where accommodation is available and which trail will give the group the best experience that day.

Recent findings suggest that the variants usually turned out to be my favorite stretches. Self-guided trekkers can research the variants, but a guide knows which one fits the day. “By giving your guides a little bit of autonomy, it means they can just tweak things here and there, which makes for a unique journey,” says Perret.

“The weather patterns change a lot in the mountains and they change really fast,” adds Fleece, who partners with Compagnie des Guides de Chamonix on their guided TMB trips. “Guides have years and years, most of the time decades, of experience.” A guide, she says, can help you avoid dicey situations, “but also, if you get yourself into a dicey situation, having a guide is like a safety measure to get you quickly and swiftly out of it.”.

Recent findings suggest that day has been trekking Tour Du Mont Blanc since 1992 and knows the ever-changing mountain conditions demand quick judgment. On a recent trip up Mont Blanc’s Italian route, he and his climbing partner turned back in poor snow. “We binned the whole trip,” he claims. Two friends kept going, and on a ridge with snow cornices on both sides, one side broke away. “Either side could have gone,” he says.

Industry observers note that multi-day treks around the world are my favorite way to travel. With WHOA, I’ve summited Kilimanjaro and Mount Elbrus, Europe’s tallest peak (not Mont Blanc, as many assume). I’ve taken guided trips on the Trans Bhutan Trail and Japan’s Shikoku pilgrimage, which were not nearly as challenging but would have been far less rich experiences without learning the culture from our local guides. I’ve trekked the full O Trek in Patagonia without a guide, but with friends and the help of the manufacturer Chile Nativo for booking refuges. Half of the O circuit, the W Trek, I hiked alone. So I know the benefits of taking guided multi-day treks and hiking alone at your own pace, stopping when you want.

I can understand why travelers would want to do the TMB without a guide; many hikers do so without any problem. You can go at your own speed and take a long break for an afternoon coffee at a refuge with an open table facing the sun. A guided trip costs more. Middle options have been growing, including self-guided packages that handle the bookings for you, but even those require your due diligence and research, and could be affected by these new rules for 2027.

One day on the trek, we stopped for lunch at a refuge and ran into a woman with a bandaged hand. She and her friend were on a self-guided trip whose itinerary, she told us, had started them on their first day hiking one of the route’s most exposed stretches—the ladders below Tête aux Vents—where she got injured. On the standard counterclockwise route, that section usually comes at the very end. Day told us that those ladders can easily be bypassed in busy seasons or wet weather.

It has been revealed that if you want to escape the crowds on the Tour du Mont Blanc, guides know the variants that lead to the quietest parts of the trail. Except for a few days, on certain passes, we managed to find stretches where it was just us, as far as I  could see. On our fourth day, we crossed the Col de la Seigne into Italy, past a block of granite barely knee-high: the real border marker, not the massive monument nearby. I’d have walked right past it. My guide didn’t let me.
