You’ve Heard “Be Bold, Start Cold.” But How Cold is Too Cold?

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1153 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Backpacker

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, hike long enough and you’ll inevitably hear the phrase, “Be Bold, Start Cold.” It’s catchy, easy to remember and generally good advice for anyone starting out early in the morning.
  • Sources indicate that but how cold is too cold?
  • When I asked Mike Tipton, a professor of human and applied physiology at the University of Portsmouth, about the old mountaineering phrase, he generally agreed with the principal but thought it needed a bit more nuance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: Alex Ratson/Getty Images).

In a recent development, hike long enough and you’ll inevitably hear the phrase, “Be Bold, Start Cold.” It’s catchy, easy to remember and generally good advice for anyone starting out early in the morning. On its surface, it’s simple: Don’t bother wearing a ton of layers you’ll take off the first fifteen minutes into your walk. Starting a little colder means skipping the first half mile shed and letting your body naturally warm up to its resting active temperature.

Sources indicate that but how cold is too cold? How do you tell the difference between a chill that’ll wear off by the first switchback and a sign you should’ve kept your jacket on? Does the first fifteen minutes warming up do more harm than good?

When I asked Mike Tipton, a professor of human and applied physiology at the University of Portsmouth, about the old mountaineering phrase, he generally agreed with the principal but thought it needed a bit more nuance.

According to recent reports, tipton has spent four decades studying how the body regulates its temperature, and part of his research looks at what happens to hands and feet during prolonged exposure to cold. His studies have informed the British Royal Navy’s approach to cooling overheated officers, and he’s worked with the U.S. Coast Guard to develop a model that estimates how long someone lost at sea might survive in cold water.

Sources indicate that his advice for hikers was simple: have a smart layering strategy. He didn’t take concern with “Be Bold,” but thought hikers should take more care when it comes to starting cold.

Industry observers note that so how do you tell whether you’re underdressed or overprepared? We talked to Tipton, Appalachian Mountain Club guide Marielle Fibish, and western North Carolina search and rescue team member Nancy East about what to wear for the first mile of a winter hike, how to tell when it’s time to add or shed a layer, and when you’re better off starting warm.

Industry observers note that for East, a good starting point is how you feel while you’re waiting for a hiking partner to lace up their boots. Can you stand around comfortably for a few minutes? “It’s the type of chill that fresh clothes from the dryer would immediately quell,” she states.

Tipton suggests paying attention to your hands. As your body cools, blood flow to your fingers decreases, which can make something as simple as working a zipper harder. In his view, “the ideal place to be is where your extremities feel warm, but you’re not producing vast amounts of sweat.”.

In a recent development, once you’re walking, pay attention to which way things are headed. Is that slight chill wearing off, or are your fingers getting colder with every switchback?

“If my hands are getting cold, I’m shivering, or I’m not generating enough body heat to feel comfortable after several minutes of hiking, I’ll add a layer,” East indicates.

It has been revealed that when Fibish gets dressed for a winter hike in the White Mountains, she checks the forecast, then dresses as though it’s about 10°F warmer. Say it’s 20°F at the trailhead. Fibish dresses the way she would for a walk in 30°F weather. The puffy, shell, and extra mittens are all coming with her. They just get to ride in her bag for the first mile.

One mistake Fibish sees is hikers reaching for the same outfit they’d wear to the ski hill.

“Insulated snow pants and jackets are great for downhill skiing and making snowmen, but they can be too warm for other outdoor winter activities like hiking or Nordic skiing,” she says. For hiking, she builds her outfit around a close-fitting wool top and bottoms, with hiking or soft-shell pants over the base layer. A separate fleece gives her some warmth she can shed on the first climb without losing her protection from the wind.

Fibish also thinks about who’s coming along. If you’re breaking trail for the group, you might be glad you left your fleece in your pack. If you tend to run cold and expect to spend some of that first mile waiting for friends, you might want to keep it on. Give yourself five or ten minutes of walking, Fibish indicates, and you’ll have a better sense of how well you guessed.

For Fibish, the first cue to lose a layer is a little tingle of warmth building under her clothes. Sometimes slipping off her hat or hiking in glove liners is enough. On a sustained climb, she might stop to take off her fleece. As Tipton explains, your working muscles produce heat. Taking off a layer lets more of that heat escape into the air, so your body can regulate its core temperature with less sweating.

Your hands can tell you when it’s time to add a layer, too. As your body cools, Tipton explains, blood vessels near the skin narrow to conserve heat in your core. That leaves less warm blood flowing to your fingers. East pays attention when her hands start getting colder, even if she’s still walking. She’ll also pull on a layer if she starts to shiver or if several minutes of hiking haven’t warmed her up. “I don’t wait until I’m genuinely cold to do something about it,” she says.

Industry observers note that A snack break is one layer change you can see coming. Once you stop climbing, your muscles produce less heat, but sweat evaporating from your damp shirt keeps cooling you. If the wind picks up at the top, East pulls on a fleece or puffy, followed by a windproof layer, before she settles in to eat. Jacket first, sandwich second.

East likes to know what those first ten minutes of walking are going to look like. If it’s especially cold, wet, or windy, she’ll start a little warmer. Same goes for an exposed stretch of trail: If the climb starts somewhere on the other side of a windy meadow, you’ve still got the meadow to cross. You can take your jacket off when you get into an area with more coverage.

So is “be bold, start cold” good advice? If you’re about to head uphill and you know you’ll be peeling off your fleece by the first switchback, sure. If you’re already cold standing there, you can keep it on and proposal to stop a few minutes up the trail.

On early starts in the Himalayas, Tipton’s group would stop five minutes up the trail so everyone could adjust their layers. It’s advice worth taking. Pick a spot a few minutes up the trail while everyone’s still gearing up. That way, nobody has to be the first to ask, “Mind if I stop and take this thing off?”.

East has her own version of the phrase: “Start cool, but don’t stay cold.”.

#205207. I Started Surfing at 52 and It Helped Me Survive Cancer

I Started Surfing at 52 and It Helped Me Survive Cancer

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1345 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outsideonline

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • “How soon after surgery can I start surfing again?”.
  • That was the first thing I asked my surgeon upon learning I had aggressive breast cancer that required a double mastectomy.
  • According to recent reports, fourteen months, three surgeries, and 21 rounds of chemotherapy and immunotherapy infusions later, I have paddled out more than 100 times.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The author surfing (Photo: Matthew Berridge).

“How soon after surgery can I start surfing again?”.

That was the first thing I asked my surgeon upon learning I had aggressive breast cancer that required a double mastectomy.

According to recent reports, fourteen months, three surgeries, and 21 rounds of chemotherapy and immunotherapy infusions later, I have paddled out more than 100 times. I’m convinced that surfing through cancer treatment saved my sanity, and possibly my life.

According to recent reports, I grew up about as far from the ocean as you can get, in the Midwest. I moved to Northern California after college and fell in love with the Pacific Ocean. Every time I went to the beach, I was fixated on watching surfers—but never thought I could join them because I was too scared to try. And once I started a family, that dream moved further out of reach.

It has been revealed that fast-forward to the COVID 2020 pandemic lockdown when the public pool where I swam on a Masters swim team was shut down. I started doing laps in the San Francisco Bay with friends. I’d always been terrified of open water swimming, but after a year of braving the Bay’s chilly, choppy waters every morning, I decided it was time to try surfing. I was already wearing a (three-millimeter triathlon) wetsuit.

In a recent development, I was 52, the age when menopause, graying hair, and wrinkles can make women feel invisible. My kids had just left home for college. I needed something big to fill that hole in my life. I took a surf lesson, and was hooked immediately. On the drive home from the beach, I bought a hooded, five-millimeter wetsuit and booties, and started surfing several mornings a week, collecting phone numbers of women I met in the lineup and parking lot.

After decades of giving everything I had to everyone around me—work colleagues, kids, husband, dogs, parents, sisters—surfing was just for me.

Soon I had built a community of women surfers aged 25 to 75 to join me for dawn patrol sessions at our break north of San Francisco and surf trips to Mexico, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, San Diego, and Santa Cruz.

Surfing made me feel strong and beautiful. So I didn’t want to give that up four years later as I faced down cancer.

Seeking guidance on how to surf through surgery recovery and treatment, I posted a message on the Facebook “Women Who Surf” group of 39,000: “I just got diagnosed with breast cancer and am looking for other women surfers who surfed through chemo, and surfed after a double mastectomy.”.

Sources indicate that A hundred women weighed in with personal experience of cancer and surfing. Most hadn’t surfed during surgery recovery or chemotherapy due to doctors’ orders, infection risk, weak immune systems, limited mobility, fatigue, and weakness.

But one woman told me to go for it: Melanie Ezell, a 42-year-old big wave surfer, based in Oahu, who surfed through ovarian cancer. She became my role model, inspiring me to paddle out as soon as I could.

Recent findings suggest that that long-awaited day came after being grounded on land for seven weeks following my double mastectomy. It was three days after my first chemotherapy infusion when my plastic surgeon declared my chest incisions adequately healed. I drove immediately to the beach, paddled out, and felt triumphant when I caught my first wave of the session.

And I kept paddling out through the remaining 11 rounds of chemotherapy.

In a recent development, on days when the swell was big and I was weak with fatigue, I’d claw through the impact zone after riding a wave, leaving my arms drained of power and lungs gasping for air. Once safely outside breaking waves, I’d rest on my board and let sets roll past until my breathing slowed. Still, being in the ocean felt like an antidote to the toxic drugs coursing through my veins. I loved watching the birds and seals, scanning the horizon for incoming sets, paddling into a rising wave, feeling its energy connect with my board.

Sometimes those sessions lasted only an hour because of my reduced stamina. But they always left me feeling stoked and alive, adjectives easily lost when you spend Tuesday afternoons hooked up to an IV bag pumping the sledgehammer drug Taxol into a port in your chest.

After my last chemotherapy session, I started ten rounds of targeted immunotherapy infusions (which I just concluded this month) and began posting GoPro videos on Instagram and Facebook of me surfing bald to inspire other women. I wanted them to see what it looks like when breast cancer takes your breasts and hair, but not your identity.

Women from around the world reached out to share their own stories: Ellen McLaughlin, a 54-year-old massage therapist and mom surfing through rectal cancer in the chilly waters at the Oregon-California border; 32-year-old Lottie Bakewell from Cornwall, England, surfing through breast cancer and the demands of caring for her one-year-old son and three-year-old daughter; Belen Kimble, a 48-year-old former professional longboarder, World Surf League commentator, surf performance coach, and single mom in Latest South Wales, Australia, surfing through breast cancer; and Caroline Wilhelm, a 55-year-old surfer and competitor from Los Angeles who took my cue to keep surfing through her breast cancer.

Backed by growing research showing that physical activity during cancer treatment offsets chemotherapy side effects and improves recovery and resilience, my little cohort of surfing cancer patients proves the ocean is not just a sanctuary, but an active prescription for healing.

But you don’t have to be a surfer to reap the benefits of physical activity during cancer. A fresh study of 45,530 women published in the Journal of the National Cancer Institute in September 2026 confirmed what my surf sisters and I already knew: regular exercise gives women going through breast cancer the strength to bounce back more fully and reclaim our lives after treatment. The study followed women for 15 years with data from the Women’s Health Initiative and found that keeping up physical activity and healthy habits prior to a cancer diagnosis acts as a powerful buffer against the physical toll of cancer treatments.

The trick is to start with small amounts of exercise and work with your care team on a game proposal to get active.

It has been revealed that “Even if you are not an exerciser, you can still start an exercise regimen during chemotherapy,” said my oncologist Eva Thomas, MD, from Kaiser Permanente Oakland in California, who encouraged and cheered on my surfing during chemotherapy. “It sounds counter-intuitive, but women tell me that when they push themselves to exercise, they feel better. Mood is better, sleep is better, energy is increased, and body aches are reduced.”.

In 2022, the American Society of Clinical Oncology released the first-ever exercise guidelines based on more than 100 clinical trials examining the link between exercise and cancer treatment. For anyone going through cancer who wants to get active, the American College of Sports Medicine created a step-by-step guide in 2024 with research benefits and resources. It outlines a path to get started.

My own path began years before cancer, as a young woman fixated on surfing, who waited decades to act upon her dream.

Looking back, I see that my surfing community—and the strength and identity it gave me—helped me to charge forward through the scariest chapter of my life. The takeaway lesson is useful for all women and men facing challenges: Don’t delay trying something new and scary. It may end up transforming, and saving, you.

Danielle Cass lives with her husband in Northern California, where they raised their 26-year-old son, 23-year-old daughter, and dogs. When she’s not surfing with friends, she leads Responsible AI enablement at Microsoft. A two-minute short film about her midlife entry into surfing Learning to Surf at 52 screened at the 2022 San Diego Surf Festival. Follow her surfing through cancer adventures on Instagram @danielle.cass and Substack Danielle Rides the Cancer Wave.

Smartwool Active Fleece Wind Headband.

Black Diamond Astro 300-R Headlamp.

There’s nothing more delightful than rummaging around in an oversized sock to find a piece of backpacking gear you never knew you needed. Even if your giftee isn’t overwhelmed with joy (we’re sure they will be), these micro-gifts won’t set you back like an expensive, ill-fitting sleeping bag might. From energy chews to our current favorite pocket knife, here are ten backpacker-tested stocking stuffers, all small enough to fit into a hipbelt pocket.

It has been revealed that hydration and electrolytes are a stacked category, but we love that Tailwind uses easy-to-drink, naturally-flavored mixes instead of unpronounceable ingredients. The 25-serving bulk bag is a good economical choice, but if single-serving packets are more convenient, you can opt for a variety pack instead. For super sweaty hikers, Saltt drink mixes add a dose of sodium to the blend without making it taste like seawater.

Industry observers note that hiking hard in the heat can be a recipe for an upset stomach, but hikers still have to eat enough to power their miles. Skratch’s energy chews are some of the easiest to get down thanks to the varied texture of the sour sugar coating and punchy flavors. Choose between caffeinated and non-caffeinated varieties, all with easy-to-digest carbs for a quick boost of energy that doesn’t entail gnawing on a dense protein bar.

A headband might not seem like a thrilling gift, but no one is ever sad they threw it into their pack. Smartwool’s version is warm and wicking, blocking brisk winds around the forehead with a windproof panel and extra width around the ears for coverage. This is the perfect accessory for chilly-but-not-frigid hikes where a beanie is overkill, but the wind is turning your forehead into an ice cube.

In a recent development, leatherman might be best known for its ranch-ready multitools, but it also has a lovely line of reliable, lightweight pocket knives. The Skeletool KB weighs just over one ounce, has a built-in bottle opener, and a tensioned belt clip for securing to a pocket or an interior flap on your pack. We’ve carried this for weeks at a time without seeing any dulling or corrosion. If you want to go big, you can also spring for a high-end Benchmade Bugout Knife, which weighs 1.85 ounces and has a range of customization options.

According to recent reports, remember being a kid and groaning when you got socks for Christmas? Those days are long gone—we don’t know any hiker who isn’t thrilled to unwrap a fresh pair of wool socks. These trail-ready socks have a moderate amount of cushioning and structure for support without feeling compressive. Made with 75-percent merino, they also have excellent odor-resistance and softness while still holding their shape.

HydraPak has made impressive strides in its line of ultralight, packable filters in the past few years. This filter-and-bottle combination uses their flagship soft flask with one of our favorite hollow-fiber filters. The flow rate stays strong and fast for longer than other similar styles, and the tough, seam-welded TPU bottle can withstand a whole lot of squeezing. The wide mouth makes it easy to fill, and hikers can either squeeze it into a larger bottle for drinking water or drink directly from the filter.

Sources indicate that black Diamond nailed it with this headlamp. The Astro 300 offers an excellent combination of low weight (just 2.65 ounces), night-hiker-approved 300-lumen output, and a conveniently integrated rechargeable battery, all at a reasonable price. It’s highly waterproof and durable for long, rugged outings, and the single button is easy to press while wearing gloves. The only downside is that it doesn’t include a red light. If that’s an concern, Nitecore’s UT27 MCT Pro 800 is more expensive, but weighs the same and comes with a red light option.

Though it gets less press than rolled ankles and bad knees, skin chafing is the sneaky destroyer of many good days on the trail. Keep your hiker’s inner thighs safe with a stick of Squirrel’s Nut Butter, which has a trimmed-down formula limited to natural ingredients like coconut oil, cocoa butter, and Vitamin E oil. It glides on smoothly, and each application lasts several hours. Fast-packers and people in more humid environments might also appreciate Run Slick, which has a roll-on formula that is among the most sweat-resistant we’ve ever tested.

It has been revealed that even the most weight-conscious backpacker will spare a few grams in the food bag for instant coffee. Alpine Start dissolves in a flash in hot water, and can even be shaken up without gritty residue in colder water for iced coffee vibes. The brand uses single-origin beans from farms in Colombia, and each packet is perfect for 8-10 ounces of water.

It has been revealed that wired headphones might be a technological relic, but for backpackers, the trend never died. We love the convenience of having one less thing to charge on the trail, and this pair from Skullcandy has excellent sound quality for a reasonable price. They’re also durable: The cords on our pair have survived over a month of daily use on-trail without separating. If you’re looking to splurge, Bose recently updated its flagship wired earbuds, and the bump in price gets you better noise-canceling and a clear in-line microphone for ordering pizza to the trailhead.

Congress Just Voted to Redraw Yosemite National Park Boundaries. The Bill Is Heading to Trump’s Desk.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The famous Tunnel View at Yosemite (Photo: Kenny McCartney/Getty Images).
  • A new law is heading to President Trump’s desk that would shift Yosemite’s boundaries by consolidating land between the National Park Service (NPS) and the National Forest System.
  • On November 18, Congress passed the Ackerson Meadow Land Interchange Act, a bill co-signed by Democratic U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The famous Tunnel View at Yosemite (Photo: Kenny McCartney/Getty Images).

A new law is heading to President Trump’s desk that would shift Yosemite’s boundaries by consolidating land between the National Park Service (NPS) and the National Forest System.

On November 18, Congress passed the Ackerson Meadow Land Interchange Act, a bill co-signed by Democratic U.S. Senator Alex Padilla and Republican U.S. Representative Tom McClintock, both from California.

If the president signs it into law, the Ackerson Meadow Land Interchange Act will transfer 160 acres of Stanislaus National Forest land to the NPS for management as part of Yosemite. Another 170 acres of Yosemite National Park land will be transferred to the U.S. Forest Service (USFS) for management as part of Stanislaus National Forest.

Sources indicate that the decision comes after a flurry of debate following announcements for public land swaps and transfers. An August report alleged that the NPS was attempting to execute a land exchange within Yosemite for a private road, which reportedly would have given property within park boundaries to a Nevada-based real estate manufacturer. Then, in September, Major League Baseball approached the Trump administration about hosting a game at Grand Teton National Park in northwest Wyoming.

Lawmakers say the Ackerson Meadow decision will address a problem in federal land management in the Sierra Nevada: the checkerboard of boundary lines. In 2016, the Trust for Public Land bought the 400-acre Ackerson Meadow parcel and gifted it to Yosemite. However, the chunk was almost completely surrounded by the Stanislaus National Forest with very little contiguous border to the park itself, lawmakers said.

“Ackerson Meadow is one of the most critical wildlife corridors in our state, yet the current configuration of the region puts habitat conservation at risk,” Padilla remarked in a statement. “This land transfer is a simple and beneficial exchange that will help protect endangered wildlife, mitigate wildfire threats, and sustain our rural economy.”.

According to recent reports, jackie McGuinness, Padilla’s communications director, told Outside that the agreement will change Yosemite’s boundaries. A map McGuinness sent shows the park boundaries shifting to the east, filling in a checkerboard pattern left blocked out by the previous perimeter lines.

In a recent development, USFS manages land ranchers use for livestock grazing on national forests and grasslands, while the NPS restricts most of these operations within park boundaries. The land exchange between the two agencies eliminates confusion caused by the jurisdictional split, McClintock mentioned in a U.S. House floor statement on September 14.

According to recent reports, “The proposed land exchange would make that cooperative approach easier by eliminating the confusion caused by split jurisdiction,” he said. “Ranchers need to know where their permits apply, where infrastructure can be maintained, and who is responsible for decisions affecting their operations.”.

It’s unclear whether or when Trump intends to sign the bill into law.

The Terminus of the CDT is Now Behind a Border Wall. Here’s What Hikers Can Expect

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (601 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Backpacker

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the southern terminus of the Continental Divide Trail has changed a lot in the last year.
  • Now, though, the monument stands between two imposing 30-foot border walls at the moment under construction, in a National Defense Area (NDA).
  • In a recent development, in November, Teresa Martinez, the executive director of the CDT Coalition (CDTC), and Audra Labert, the CDTC director of communications, traveled to the southern terminus.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the southern terminus of the Continental Divide Trail has changed a lot in the last year. The granite obelisk once stood in the open Chihuahuan Desert, in a remote area visited by few except hikers either starting or ending their journeys. The dirt road approaching it, Commodore Road, was unmaintained and required high-clearance vehicles, limiting access and traffic.

Now, though, the monument stands between two imposing 30-foot border walls at the moment under construction, in a National Defense Area (NDA). Government contractors graded and widened the road from 8 feet to 24 feet to accommodate construction vehicles. For now, hikers can still enter the NDA with permission and touch the monument—whether they’re starting northbound or ending their CDT hike. However, security guards will eventually usher them away, out of the construction zone.

In a recent development, in November, Teresa Martinez, the executive director of the CDT Coalition (CDTC), and Audra Labert, the CDTC director of communications, traveled to the southern terminus. Neither had been there since construction began in early 2026.

According to recent reports, “We wanted to see on the ground what was actually happening and what people were experiencing,” Martinez told Backpacker. She described the scene as “surreal.”.

Industry observers note that arriving at the terminus monument, Martinez and Labert watched as two hikers approached in the distance. The two women, trail names Geisha Girl and Fearless, marched toward them, border walls standing on both sides. In an emotional moment, the teary-eyed hikers walked right up to the monument.

It has been revealed that “I think if they hadn’t been able to put their hands on the physical monument, even though it was between the two barriers, it would have been devastating,” Martinez stated. “The importance of having access to that now while it’s under construction is so fundamental.”.

It has been revealed that while these changes are striking to someone like Martinez, who has visited this terminus hundreds of times during her work with the non-profit trail organization, she notes she sees a silver lining. The construction traffic is annoying, loud, disruptive, and changes the experience of finishing or starting your CDT hike in a quiet corner of the desert. But the improvements to Commodore Road greatly increase access to the trail’s southern terminus.

Recent findings suggest that “Building a road invites more people, which means more people can get there, which is a beautiful thing. They can drive their loved ones to the trail and pick them up from the trail much easier than it ever has been,” she remarked. But at the same time, the improvements make it feel less remote, and could make it significantly busier. “So it’s bittersweet,” she said.

Sometime “in the near future,” Martinez said the terminus monument will be moved out of the NDA. Then, the CDTC will create a latest one with accurate longitude and latitude markers. She sees that as an opportunity to rethink how the monument will be dedicated and to include indigenous voices that weren’t involved when the original monument was dedicated in 1974.

Asked what hikers should expect when approaching the southern terminus of the CDT, Martinez paused thoughtfully.

It has been revealed that “I think they should be prepared for an amazing experience in one of the most beautiful places on the planet,” she said. “But you’re going to see this infrastructure now that didn’t exist before. And I would ask people to lean into the good stuff and then also use that moment as an opportunity to reflect on how the experience is making them feel.”.

Industry News: Skiing Takes a Toll on Your Knees. Here’s the Muscle You Need to Strengthen, According to an Orthopedic Surgeon.

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1068 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outsideonline

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • (Photo: Monster walk exercise: Erstudiostok/Getty; Design: Ayana Underwood/Canva).
  • Strong legs are essential for skiing without injury.
  • Industry observers note that that means the smaller guys often get neglected.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: Monster walk exercise: Erstudiostok/Getty; Design: Ayana Underwood/Canva).

Strong legs are essential for skiing without injury. But many traditional strength training programs focus on the bigger muscles in your lower half, including the quads, hamstrings, and gluteus maximus (your largest butt muscle).

Industry observers note that that means the smaller guys often get neglected. And one small guy in particular, the gluteus medius, which forms part of your side butt, is worth paying attention to if you actually want to reduce your risk of knee pain and injury this winter.

Industry observers note that because ACL tears are among the most common ski injuries, Dr. Gregory Lichtman, an orthopedic surgeon in northern California and a physician for the U.S. women’s ski team, puts heavy emphasis on strengthening the glute medius. In his view, it’s one of the most important muscles for staying safe and skiing well.

Unfortunately, even high-level athletes can have a weak glute medius, according to Lichtman. That’s because unlike the quads, hamstrings, calves, and glute max—which can naturally get strong from activities like road running and hill climbing—the glute medius typically needs to be intentionally strengthened.

Read on to learn why this small muscle is so important, Lichtman’s favorite way to strengthen it, and other essential fitness tips for injury prevention.

The glute medius is a small muscle on your outer hip that fires up when you bring your leg out to the side, a motion known as hip abduction. It also helps control the knee by preventing it from caving inward (a position known as valgus) as you perform various movements. And it assists you in balancing on one leg, which is vital when loading your downhill ski, Lichtman notes.

According to recent reports, in skiing, if you get into the back seat (meaning, you shift your body weight backward, instead of staying centered over your skis) and the knee goes into valgus, the tibia can internally rotate, “and that’s where the ACL tears occur,” Lichtman says. Even if you don’t get a full-blown ACL tear, going into valgus when you ski can contribute to patellofemoral pain syndrome, a fancy term for pain at the front of the kneecap, Lichtman says.

By strengthening the glute medius, you can make it more resistant to valgus in the first place, which decreases your chances of both ACL tears and general knee pain.

There are also performance benefits: “A strong gluteus medius also really allows you to stand on your downhill ski a little bit more aggressively and really make a more aggressive turn,” Lichtman notes. That’s because when you place most of your weight on your downhill ski (the one that’s closest to the bottom of the hill), your G-forces will want to throw you down the mountain. But having a strong glute medius, in addition to strong quads and core muscles, helps form a strong pillar on your outer hip, which “really allows you to withstand those G-forces the best,” Lichtman says.

One of the classic ways to target the glute medius is to strap on ankle weights, lie on your side, and lift and lower your top leg. Lichtman says. This exercise can absolutely strengthen your glute medius, but it’s not Lichtman’s go-to. That’s because it primarily just isolates that muscle and doesn’t mimic how we move in sports.

In a recent development, A better bet, Lichtman says, is to focus on exercises that simultaneously activate the gluteus medius and other muscle groups because that better resembles how we use this muscle during athletics. His favorite exercise that ticks that box? The monster walk. Not only does this move really fire up the gluteus medius, but it also works the core, hamstrings, quads, and glute max, he says.

Industry observers note that incorporate this exercise into your workouts three days a week, with at least one day off between sessions so the muscle has the downtime it needs to recover and build back stronger. To stave off boredom and also work different parts of your hips and quads, incorporate different variations of the monster walk throughout the week. For example, instead of stepping straight out to the side, step forward and back, or diagonally forward and diagonally back. As long as you have good form and keep your legs spread apart so that you feel tension from the band the whole time, “all directions can be effective,” Lichtman says.

Recent findings suggest that lichtman suggests doing monster walks during both pre-season and throughout ski season. “One of the big pitfalls is that we will all get ready for ski season, and then taper off our dry land training,” he explains. “If you’re one of the fortunate few who can ski five or six days a week, you’re probably getting enough exercise, and you probably don’t want to stress your body out any more than that. But for those of us who are skiing two to three days a week, finding some time to do some cross-training and continue to work on our core and our hip abductor strength is really key because those are the less commonly used muscles during skiing.”.

Once this exercise becomes easy, level up the challenge by using a stronger resistance band.

A strong glute medius can keep you safe on the slopes. But it’s not the only fitness-related aspect of injury prevention.

It has been revealed that A strong core and quads, along with good overall endurance, are also key. That’s because one of the essential components of an ACL tear pattern in skiing is getting kicked into the back seat. And while the gluteus medius helps guard against knee valgus in this position, it doesn’t prevent you from getting into the back seat in the first place, Lichtman explains. What does help? Having strong core and quad muscles, plus overall endurance. This trifecta, Lichtman claims, is “fundamental” to staying out of the back seat.

On the endurance front, the goal is to be as fresh after lunch as you are after breakfast, Lichtman says. “Fatigue is definitely a risk factor for ACL tears,” he says, explaining that fatigued skiers more frequently get into the back seat and sustain injuries than those who aren’t zapped. So make sure your dryland training doesn’t just focus on lifting weights: “A balance of endurance and strength training is integral for a skier preparing for ski season,” Lichtman says.

  • Recent findings suggest that but not everyone can access hiking right out their front door.
  • Recent findings suggest that with that in mind, we’ve put together a list of the best places for hikers to holiday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: Photos from Terry's photostream via Flickr Creative Commons).

Recent findings suggest that but not everyone can access hiking right out their front door. So why not turn your holiday break into a hiking vacation? You’ll not only get to make special festive memories outside, but you can choose the geography and even the climate.

Recent findings suggest that with that in mind, we’ve put together a list of the best places for hikers to holiday. Want to spend your time traipsing through deserts, among cacti and palm trees? We’ve got you covered. Looking for a more traditional experience, with snowy trails and evergreen forests? No problem. And, of course, if you like long walks on the beach and among tropical rainforests, we’ve got just the places for you.

Why it’s a great holiday town: Mild weather, southwestern culture, diverse landscapes, and amazing food December temps: 40-65℉ What to expect: Both desert and mountain landscapes with rocky, sandy terrain, and no snow.

For those hikers who’d rather decorate a saguaro cactus than a lodgepole pine, Tucson, Arizona is calling your name. The wildernesses around town are packed with desert flora and fauna, and crisscrossed with tons of hiking trails. This can be a tough place to explore during late spring, summer, and even into fall because it gets so scorching hot. However, in the winter, the weather is perfect for hiking, making this a prime place to spend the holidays. Beyond the trails, the food is world-renowned—Tucson has been a UNESCO City of Gastronomy for over a decade.

Why it’s a great holiday town: Fair weather, proximity to Gila National Forest and Cliff Dwellings Monument, colorful western history, and a great art scene December temps: 21-55℉ What to expect: Colder, high desert climate, with very clear weather, and tons of trails exploring the Pinos Altos and Mogollon Mountains.

Industry observers note that situated on the outskirts of the Gila National Forest, Silver City is a gateway to desert hiking adventures. The Continental Divide Trail passes nearby; City of Rocks State Park is just 30 miles east of town, and the famous Gila Cliff Dwellings National Monument is just 44 miles north. The monument area gets over 200 cloudless nights a year, making it a prime destination for winter stargazers. If you want a warm soak after your hikes, Faywood Hot Springs and Gila Hot Springs are both close to town.

Why it’s a great holiday town: Mild temperatures, direct access to Zion National Park, regional access to Bryce Canyon or Grand Canyon, and a lively restaurant and art scene December temps: 30-55℉ What to expect:  A striking red sandstone desert landscape and trails both in the park and outside of it.

It has been revealed that winter is Zion National Park’s slow season, and yet it’s just as beautiful as it is any other time of year. Springdale sits just outside the park’s eastern entrance and is a prime location for a hiking holiday basecamp. Not only will you have direct access to the national park and all of its trails, but there are also worthy routes around town that don’t require an entrance fee. And if you aren’t afraid of a day trip, Bryce Canyon is 86 miles away.

Why it’s a great holiday town: Mild temperatures, access to Lake Mead, fun holiday atmosphere, and a historic downtown December temps: 35-55℉ What to expect: Wide Mojave desert terrain with rolling hills and rocky mountains, canyons, panoramic lake views, and old mining and railroad infrastructure.

Industry observers note that the deserts of southern Nevada have a lot to offer beyond the flashing lights, casinos, and nightlife of Las Vegas. About an hour southeast of Sin City, Boulder City is a much quieter historic town that offers access to some amazing trails and outdoor recreation areas. It’s just a short drive from Boulder City to Lake Mead Recreation Area, where there are a lot of trails, walkways, and observation points. Some hikes close to town are short and approachable, while others challenge hikers with scrambles and steep climbs. The city itself is full of history; it was once an old mining town and played an crucial role in the Hoover Dam’s construction.

Why it’s a great holiday town: Mountain scenery and trails, access to Blue Ridge Parkway, and relatively mild temperatures and weather December temps: 35-55℉ What to expect: Forested mountains, waterfalls, and (potentially) snowy trails.

Within minutes of Asheville, you’ll find waterfall hikes, mountain overlooks, and plenty of access to public lands. The Blue Ridge Mountains make a beautiful backdrop for town, and an even more spectacular place to explore by trail. Asheville’s thickly wooded forests are magical to hike, with trails following icy creeks and ascending ridges to spectacular views. After your hike, the town is renowned for its craft beer scene and festive holiday light displays. If a cozy Appalachian holiday is your vibe, look no further.

Why it’s a great holiday town: Situated high in the Rocky Mountains, lively restaurant and bar scene, trails in every direction, and close to two ski resorts December temps: 12-42℉ What to expect: Cold-weather mountain hikes, snowy trails, old-growth forests, and high desert terrain.

Durango, Colorado, is a pure western mountain ski town and a genuinely cozy place to spend the holidays. The San Juan Mountains offer incredible hiking for all levels, whether you just want to stroll along a creek or climb for panoramic views of the Rockies. This region gets a lot of snow in the wintertime, so be prepared for cold weather with the right gear, knowledge, and expectations. For holiday adventurers, Durango is packed with things to do in the winter. Beyond the hiking trails, ride the historic Durango and Silverton Narrow Gauge Railroad, or go skiing at Wolf Creek or Purgatory Resorts.

Why it’s a great holiday town: Warm, subtropical winter weather, surrounded by ample inland and beach hiking, and deeply historic roots December temps: 50-70℉ What to expect: Sand dune beaches, flatland ecosystems, wetlands, and marshes.

In a recent development, st. Augustine offers a unique take on the traditional winter holiday. It’s coastal, subtropical, and offers landscapes and ecosystems you’ll only find in Florida—from swamp conservation areas to beach parks and historic forts. There are over 30 trails and walkways around St. Augustine, and it’s within an hour’s drive of six state parks. Most of the hiking is very approachable, following beaches, boardwalks, sand dunes, and mostly flat terrain. The town was settled over 450 years ago, so it’s also a great place for history buffs, and it annually hosts a Christmas parade and “Night of Lights” throughout December.

Why it’s a great holiday town: Warm, tropical weather, dramatic natural scenery, laid-back island culture, and great hiking access December temps: 65-80℉ What to expect: Lush rainforests, beautiful beaches, mountains spouting waterfalls, and the opportunity to surf substantial swells.

Sources indicate that hawaii is a famous holiday destination for obvious reasons. In the winter, the climate is pleasant; the landscape is dramatic, there are beaches a’plenty, and the hiking access is hard to beat. Waterfalls spout from the mountains, and trails wind through thick rainforest, popping out on beaches that you might have all to yourself. Hanalei, on Kauai’s North Shore, offers some of Hawaii’s best (and most diverse) hiking. Nearby are several forest reserves, Kōke’e State Park, and the Hanalei National Wildlife Refuge.

Why it’s a great holiday town: Bavarian influence, Christmas spirit, and ample winter trails to explore December temps: 15-35℉ What to expect: Snowy trails through old-growth forests and mountains, and a town that really loves to celebrate Christmas.

Tucked away in the Cascade Mountains of Washington, along the Wenatchee River, this Bavarian-influenced town is one of the best places to spend the holidays on this list. The hiking in the surrounding mountains offers access to postcard-worthy alpine lakes, waterfalls, and ridges. It ranges from strenuous and challenging to easy and mellow. You’ll want snowshoes and/or microspikes if you proposal on holidaying in Leavenworth, as the trails will likely be snowy and/or icy in places. The town is well-known for its Christmas zeal: It has a “Christmastown,” a Bavarian village that comes to life with live music, carols, ice carving, fireworks, and, of course, appearances by Santa Claus.

Tech Report: How to Make a Handprint Calendar

📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (600 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tinybeans

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, hanging around the house for the holidays?
  • According to recent reports, we love this project because there’s no right way to make one.
  • Related: How to Make a Vision Board for Kids in 2027.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, hanging around the house for the holidays? Spend an afternoon or two working on a handprint calendar for 2027. It’s an easy project anyone can complete, and little helpers will love to lend a hand or two. After all, you’ve got a long winter break to fill with activities and printables, and by New Year’s Eve, you’ll have reached the point where painting your kids’ hands sounds like a rational idea!

According to recent reports, we love this project because there’s no right way to make one. Keep it simple, or get super crafty— it’s all up to your kids’ imagination. Use the guide below to get started, and decide in advance what you’ll make out of each handprint. This is much easier to do before your little helper has paint all over their hands!

Related: How to Make a Vision Board for Kids in 2027.

Recent findings suggest that paint your kids’ hands with the selected colors and have them make a print on each piece of paper. Colored paper is also an option if you want to use white paint (see January and October). Depending on your design, you may need just one handprint, a fingerprint, or even a footprint. Be sure to wash and dry your hands between each month, and continue through the year, from January to December. If you think it doesn’t look like much, don’t worry! After each month has dried, and you add the details, it’ll look awesome.

Insider Tip: Let your kids have some input with this project. While you may have a perfect vision in mind for how to execute a gorgeous Christmas tree using their sweet little hands, they might have another idea, and that’s okay.

Now that you have all of the months ready to go (and dry!), it’s time to put your calendar together. The easiest way to go is to order a ready-made blank calendar, such as this blank wall calendar from Amazon. For under $10, you won’t have to mess with binding or stapling, or fussing with the assembly of the calendar—glue or use double-sided tape to attach your own homemade monthly pictures to the blank template and you’re good to go.

Related: New Year’s Eve Confetti Poppers You Can Make with the Kids.

It has been revealed that print out a blank 2023 calendar from Calendar Labs. One by one, place the pages behind the handprint so that when it flips upward, you’ll have the right picture and month. For example, the calendar days for January should be glued to the February picture, the calendar days for February should be glued to March, and so on.

Insider Tip: Make sure to place the calendar month on the backside and bottom of the handprint, so as you flip each month, the painted picture is positioned the correct way.

Once you’ve glued all the calendar pages to the handprints, use the laminating sleeves to seal each one. Follow the instructions on the package, and use a ruler to eliminate any air pockets or creases.

Using a hole punch, make three holes at the top of each page (the calendar month should have the holes at the top) and one hole at the bottom (this is where the calendar will hang on the wall).

Then, using string or thin twine, run a length through each of the three holes and tie it up like you would a book (it should open from the right side). That’s it! You’ll have a fun keepsake that will hang around for an entire year.

Sleep-Unders Are Honestly a Win for Everyone

📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (302 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Tinybeans

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As soon as kids hit school age, the pressure of the sleepover begins.
  • Recent findings suggest that the sleep-under brings the best elements of the sleepover and avoids the actual sleeping-over part.
  • Recent findings suggest that all the festivities are concluded just before bedtime, when parents return to swoop up their little ones and everyone heads back home to sleep in their own beds.

As soon as kids hit school age, the pressure of the sleepover begins. Whether your little one wants to host a crew of first graders in your living room (hard pass) or is being asked to sleep over at someone else’s house, there are a lot of questions that come with the milestone. Will my kid have fun? Will they sleep at all? Will they be overwhelmed? Add to that concerns surrounding safety, and it’s a tough position for parents to be in. The solution: the “sleep-under.”.

Recent findings suggest that the sleep-under brings the best elements of the sleepover and avoids the actual sleeping-over part. It’s become a trendy birthday party theme because it puts less pressure on kids and the parents hosting. How it works is that kids show up to the host house all ready for a sleepover, usually around dinner time. Guests might even arrive decked out in their coziest PJs to add to the whole sleepover vibe. The group enjoys pizza, watches a movie, plays some games, and does an activity like decorating cupcakes.

Recent findings suggest that all the festivities are concluded just before bedtime, when parents return to swoop up their little ones and everyone heads back home to sleep in their own beds. Nobody is over-tired the next day. Nobody needs to call home for a late-night pickup when they have a nightmare. No parent has to stress over whether it’s a good idea to leave their kid overnight with someone they only know from the pick-up line. No kid has to feel ashamed if they aren’t yet ready to sleep away from their parents for the night. The sleep-under side-steps all those potential concerns.

Honestly, it’s pretty genius. We just wish it were a thing when we were kids!

Breaking: 21 Easy Play Ideas for Kids (Whether You Have 5, 15, or 30 Minutes)

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1635 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tinybeans

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Between daily parenting duties, work, and navigating the current world in general, saying your days are full is probably an understatement.
  • It has been revealed that even five minutes can make a difference in a child’s emotional well-being.
  • The good news is, there are lots of ways to play that take next-to-no prep.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Between daily parenting duties, work, and navigating the current world in general, saying your days are full is probably an understatement. And while your kid’s day may be full of exploration and creativity, they can also experience a lot of anxiety, stress, and pressure. That makes it even more important to have some positive, uninterrupted time to reconnect.

It has been revealed that even five minutes can make a difference in a child’s emotional well-being. But as Randy McCoy, VP of Product & Curriculum for The Little Gym, reminds us, how long you play is less important than how often. “It’s not necessarily the ‘duration of play’ but the ‘frequency of play’ that matters most,” Mccoy claims. “If a parent can give their child their undivided attention and play with them just five minutes a day, every day, they’re on the right track.”.

The good news is, there are lots of ways to play that take next-to-no prep. Read on for 21 easy ideas to play with your kids, whether you have five minutes, 15, or more.

When you have a few minutes, whether it’s before school or after dinner, bust out these little-to-no-prep basics you can use just about anywhere.

Sources indicate that 1. Try out “Would You Rather?” kid edition. Spend a fun five minutes taking turns asking questions like, “Would you rather never eat ice cream again or get a trampoline?” or “Ride a dinosaur for 20 miles or an elephant for an hour?” The sillier the better. This also makes a great road trip game.

Sources indicate that 2. Make a dictionary dash. Grab a dictionary and choose a word at random. Read it out loud and have the kids guess what it means. If they can read, they can take turns finding words and trying to stump you.

3. Tickle your sidekick’s funny bone. Whip out brain busters or riddles that will make them laugh. Luckily, you don’t need Comedy Central writers for this one. We think your goofballs will get a kick out of our ultimate list of jokes for kids.

4. A few rounds of “We’re going on a picnic” alphabet-style will entertain the tot lot. The first player up says, “I’m going on a picnic,” then adds a tasty packable to the phrase, like an apple, apricot, or avocado. Stick with ABC order or focus on just one letter for each round.

In a recent development, 5. Play 20 questions. Have your kids guess what you’re thinking of, and keep it simple, like something you can see from where you’re standing.

6. Play a classic game of Rock, Paper, Scissors—Japanese style. It’s called Janken. Start by saying “saisho wa guu.” Then “janken pon” as you pump, before throwing on “pon.” The winning combos are still the same in this timeless, quick game you can play at home or on the go.

7. Turn yourself into a living “spot the difference” puzzle. Start with a slow model turn, then disappear and make a quick change out of sight. When you come back, your cutie’s got to spot what’s different. Did you take off a cap? Put on a scarf? Untie a shoe? Keep it easy for the tots, and kick it up a notch for older kiddos (only one earring!). Then let them have a turn trying to stump you.

8. Try out a sequencing game when the wanderlust takes hold. Name a person, place, and object, all starting with the same letter of the alphabet, then string them together like kids lining up for the school bus. “Alice from Australia loves alligators!” See how far you can get in a short amount of time.

Sources indicate that for parents, playing with our kids allows us to step out of all those daily parental duties and, as McCoy explains, build friendship between parent and child. “It provides an opportunity for you to interact with them on a different level,” he notes. “For a special moment, you step out of the ‘parent’ role and step into a playmate role.”  Take a break from your to-do list and try one of these 15-minute ideas that will thrill the kids and relax you, too.

9. Post-It style. A stack of Post-It notes and a pen are all it takes to play this short-and-sweet variation of the classic guessing game for parties. Choose someone to be “it.” Write on the Post-It note the name of a character from a book, movie, or show that your kid will recognize—it can be a famous person, someone they know, or a fictional character. Stick the note to their forehead, without letting them see what you wrote. Now take turns going around the room giving “it” clues to help them guess who is on their head.

Industry observers note that 10. Curl up with a good book. Putting out a basket of books in a central location motivates the kids to take a look through the pages when they’ve got time to spare. Add in a sweet bookmark that keeps track of time to make it count.

11. Give them their daily feels. Keep your favorite sensory bin fillers on hand (like cotton balls and dry beans), along with trinkets to bury and cups for spilling and filling. When you’ve got a short window, pull out the bin, fill ‘er up, and watch your kids dig and drizzle until it’s time to go.

12. Set up a quick cotton ball and straw race. Perfect for the kitchen table before lunch is served. Have siblings challenge each other for the pole position on a straightaway down the center of the table, or set up a simple obstacle course using cups that the kiddos have to work around. Ready, set, go!

13. Give a penny for their thoughts when they write in a journal. Setting aside a short amount of time to write (each day!) is a great way to encourage your amateur author’s creativity. Use silly or thought-provoking prompts to get them thinking, like, “The first time I tried …” or “When I get to be principal, I’ll …” or even “The craziest thing that happened today…” Write on, brother!

According to recent reports, 14. Give up the charade. Have your little monkey stay in character when you play a quick game of animal charades. No prep is necessary for this easy guessing game. Just pick your favorite animal and go for it! With each successful guess, trade places and start again. Ee-i-ee-i-o!

Whether your aim is active playtime or quiet(er) crafting time, filling a cool 30 minutes with your kids is easier than you think. It may take a bit of planning, but once the prep is done, it’s a sit-back-and-relax situation that’s well worth the time upfront.

In a recent development, 15. All things LEGO. If LEGO was the first thing that popped into your head, then we’re right there with you. They’re the forever fallback for a reason, but to hit that half-hour sweet spot, try throwing a LEGO challenge into the mix: building a car that can also work underwater, or constructing a tower that’s at least 24 inches tall. Then let your master-builder go to work.

Industry observers note that 16. Spin them right round. Ana at Babble Dabble Do has a fresh way to play with Perler beads. She puts them to work teaching science and playing tricks when these melted beauties become spinning tops. It’s just the right amount of make-and-play to fill a brief window in your busy day.

17. One for the movers and shakers. Print out (and laminate if you’re feeling bold) The Alerting Activity Game, designed by Training Happy Hearts. Keep the deck on hand to stack the odds in your favor when the kids need something to do. With simple activities like “jump up and down ten times” or “pretend to be a volcano,” it’s packed with energy-burning activities that kids can run through on their own or with you!

Recent findings suggest that 18. Bring the outside in and paint it. If snow isn’t covering your yard, go for a hunt for leaves, evergreen boughs, and sticks. Then take your findings to the craft table to fancy them up with paint. Acrylics work great for this project.

In a recent development, for activities that span the hour, the two-step Make & Play approach works well. You may want to do a little prep the day before to make it easier, like putting crafting necessities into one small bin that you can pull out to surprise the kids.

19. Wage war. Ah, the classic card game that is so simple to learn and so hard to win. It is possible that a game of war can take longer than one hour, but it rarely takes less. You do two card battles with the highest card the winner until one person has all the cards. Get the complete rules here.

Recent findings suggest that 20. Create a mini catapult. Little Bins for Little Hands has an awesome tutorial, using craft sticks and other office supplies you’re sure to have around the house. Once it’s built, set up target practice plates before letting the marshmallows fly.

It has been revealed that 21. Put on a show. Puppets never get old; they’re easy to make with an old sock, brown paper lunch bag, or even familiar characters glued to craft sticks. Whatever method you choose, spend time creating and playing with puppets when you’ve got an hour or more to spare. Be sure to stock the craft bin with all kinds of googly eyes, buttons, yarn, and doo-dads to help bring your buddies to life. Then find an old sheet or use a baby’s blanket draped over the table to create a stage. Bravo!

It’s almost 2027, yikes! Spend an afternoon focusing on dreams and goals for the year (hello, travel!) by making a vision board with the kids. From learning a new skill to going on a fantastic trip, there’s no end to the awesome things you can manifest for yourself and your family.

Mod Podge (or similar decoupaging paste).

If you can see your aspirations on a daily basis, they are more likely to become a reality. Start by writing down goals and ideas, and have your kids do the same!

Browse old magazines for words, phrases, and images representing each goal.

Use the Mod Podge to paste each clipped item onto the blank canvas. Be sure to brush a coat of gloss over each image. Don’t worry, it will dry clear!

Once it's done, your kids can decide where to hang or place their vision board, and remember, it should be a place they can see clearly!

41 Elf on the Shelf Ideas (Because You’re Gonna Need Them)

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1388 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tinybeans

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Yup, your Elf on the Shelf is about to parachute in to make your life (slightly) more challenging for the next few weeks.
  • Sources indicate that I remember when my kids were little, and they got their first elves.
  • If you have two Scout elves, this easy Elf idea is a lot of fun.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s that time again. Yup, your Elf on the Shelf is about to parachute in to make your life (slightly) more challenging for the next few weeks. Get ahead of the game and prep your bag of tricks with these brilliant ideas. From Elf on the Shelf clothes to last-minute Elf on the Shelf ideas that’ll make the whole family giggle, we’ve got enough easy Elf ideas to last you the entire holiday season.

Sources indicate that I remember when my kids were little, and they got their first elves. Not going to lie, remembering to move the thing every night was a struggle. But when I made the effort and managed to pull off even the easiest of Elf ideas, the look in their eyes was priceless.

It has been revealed that 1. Elf held captive. If you have two Scout elves, this easy Elf idea is a lot of fun. Pull out a toy train and a string, and decide which elf is going to be extra naughty by tying up the other one.

Sources indicate that 2. Proposal a hot cocoa party. This is fun on the first night or maybe on a weekend day. Get mugs, instant cocoa, and marshmallows set up in advance and settle the elves against the mugs. Snag printables for the party here.

Recent findings suggest that 3. Spell it out. Do you have Scrabble tiles or Bananagrams? Then it’s a cinch to let your elf leave a sweet message for your littles to discover the next day.

It has been revealed that 4. Caught in the act. With this easy elf idea, you’ll use a bag of M&Ms, chocolate chips, or even a box of sugar cereal, and position your elf with its backside out of the bag.

5. Exhausted elf. All those trips up to the North Pole make for one tired elf. Let your little one in red take a day off. Make them a little bed with a doll blanket and a cotton ball for a pillow.

6. Deeds worth doing. Since reporting good deeds to Santa is your elf’s duty, it’s the perfect opportunity to remind kids about the spirit of Christmas. We dig the free downloadable from Over the Big Moon.

Recent findings suggest that 7. Elf spaghetti. Whip up Buddy the Elf’s favorite dish for your little helper. Hint: this is a great idea for the night you make pasta. You’ll also need syrup (of course), marshmallows, candy, and chocolate syrup. Find out how to make a batch over at Instructables.

8. Riding the banister. Those naughty elves are always looking for an adrenaline rush! Use a Frisbee and sticky tape to get your little buddy set up at the top and ready to ride.

9. Sitting pretty. Have your elf take a seat inside your wreath or on the holiday table for a picture-perfect spot.

In a recent development, 10. Play games. Set up your elf mid-move with this adorable mini-Twister printable.

Industry observers note that 11. Window view. If you’ve got a window and a curtain rod, you’ve got a sweet spot to hang your elf. Easy-peasy.

It has been revealed that 12. Rock climbing wall. All you need is several pre-made bows to make a route for your elf.

13. Coloring elf. Take 30 seconds to scribble in a coloring book or on a printable, scatter crayons, and set up your elf. Giggles are guaranteed!

Industry observers note that 15. Zipline. This Elf on the Shelf idea is popular, but it does take a little time to set up. All you need is string or yarn, a candy cane, and a way to secure your elf to the candy cane!

It has been revealed that 16. LEGO throne. Whether you use DUPLO or LEGO, making a seat for Santa’s little helper can be done in less than five minutes.

17. Elf in the kitchen. Got a play kitchen? Then let your elf whip up something yummy.

According to recent reports, 18. On the road. With a toy car, your elf can go just about anywhere they want to go. Headed to buy a Christmas tree? Done. Want to take Wonder Woman out on a date? Totally!

19. Play Picasso. A dry-erase marker, a family photo, and a sense of humor are all you need. Give your kids beards and cat ears: See how much they laugh!

Recent findings suggest that 20. Put the elf in the freezer. Your elf sure does miss the North Pole! Give him a little time to chill.

In a recent development, 21. Toilet paper tricks. Add an elf to a roll of toilet paper and send them down the stairs. Don’t have a second level? Leave a trail of written messages down the hall instead.

22. Bath time. You don’t need a Barbie bath to let your Elf soak aching bones— a plastic bowl or storage container will do the trick. Add marshmallows for bubbles, and you’re set.

23. Gone fishing. Your kids will love waking up to find the elf “fishing” for goldfish crackers in the bathroom sink.

According to recent reports, 24. Story time. Position the elf with a favorite holiday book and a captivated audience.

25. Hanging by a limb. Any elf will feel right at home when dangling from a branch of the Christmas tree.

26. Spa day. Wrap your elf in a paper towel, give them cucumber eye patches, and just like that, it’s a spa day.

27. Puzzle play. Settling your elf in for the night with a puzzle is easy and fun.

28. Paper bag race. Take those lunch bags that have been cluttering your drawer and collect a few stuffies. Then, stage a sack race-style scene across your dining room table or kitchen island.

In a recent development, 29. Elfie selfie. Position your elf in front of the family laptop and snap a picture. Just be forewarned, if it’s a laptop you use, you’ll need to get it set back up before the kids get home from school.

According to recent reports, 30. Sweet snow angels. It’s not quite as cold down here as it is at the North Pole. When your elf gets antsy for chilly weather, make them a personal snow angel. You can use flour (but it’s messy), sprinkles, or rice, which is my personal favorite because it’s the easiest to clean up!

Sources indicate that 31. All wrapped up. Give your elf the scissors, tape, and wrapping paper. Scatter shredded paper and tape around, and it’ll be like they were caught in the act of wrapping up Santa’s gifts!

32. Elf making popcorn. Someone’s ready for family movie night!

Sources indicate that 33. Don’t move the elf. Well, it looks like your kids were so well-behaved that no North Pole reporting was needed. It’s also the perfect excuse for one of those nights you forget to move them.

According to recent reports, 34. Cards, anyone? Didn’t you know elves love to play games? They do, and they love to be caught mid-game.

35. A Stuck Elf. This is a super-easy elf idea, and you don’t even need the message board to pull it off. Just grab a mason jar or an empty water bottle and a prominent place to display your elf’s tight situation.

Recent findings suggest that 36. S’more to love. Some toothpicks, roasted marshmallows, chocolate squares, graham crackers, and tea lights are all you need to set up this cozy and easy elf idea.

37. Read all about it. Prop them up on a favorite Christmas story or beloved book.

According to recent reports, 38. Caught red-handed. Have your elf stage a scene of questionable actions and tape up the area with crepe paper.

Recent findings suggest that 39. Photo editor. They can’t help but make mischief, and marking up a festive photo is a silly way to say, “Elf wuz here.”.

Industry observers note that 40. Riding dinos. If you’ve got a plastic dinosaur (T. rex preferred), then you’ve got what you need to give your elf a prehistoric ride.

Recent findings suggest that 41. Send the Elf back to the North Pole. Possibly one of our favorite easy elf ideas: on Christmas Morning, make sure they’re out of sight, and of course, leave a note.

The Best Way to Avoid a Meltdown When iPad Time Is Over

💡 Key Takeaways
  • We can already feel the tension spreading through our bodies: It’s time to put away the iPad, but there is a small person who is almost certainly going to lose their mind when you tell them.
  • Chelsey Hauge-Zavaleta recently shared her method for successfully ending iPad time, and it combines a little bit of the two approaches above with some voice modulation and sensory input.
  • It has been revealed that A few things to note about this method.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We can already feel the tension spreading through our bodies: It’s time to put away the iPad, but there is a small person who is almost certainly going to lose their mind when you tell them. Whether you resort to a countdown timer or go the “this is your last show” route, it’s pretty much always a struggle.

Perhaps you need a latest strategy. Parenting coach Dr. Chelsey Hauge-Zavaleta recently shared her method for successfully ending iPad time, and it combines a little bit of the two approaches above with some voice modulation and sensory input.

It has been revealed that A few things to note about this method. Using language like “We have one more song” instead of “This is our last song before we leave for school” focuses on what the child is doing now versus what you are doing in the future. It’s easier for kids to accept the transition this way.

“Melodic intonation” is when you use a sing-songy voice to make a statement. It helps kids notice what you are saying and acknowledge it. Take a look at Miss Rachel and a lot of the other preschool-focused programming, and you’ll see it employed often. Using melodic intonation for the phrase “iPad is all done” helps to signal the transition for the child.

Sources indicate that it’s vital to remember that even when using a technique like this, it will take you doing it the same way over and over several times before your child catches on and gets with the program. If they have a meltdown, don’t engage; stay calm; and move on.

If you don’t give a toddler something to do, they’ll find their own source of entertainment—and that can be a terrifying prospect (you know the feeling if you’ve suddenly noticed the house is too quiet only to find that they’ve somehow given themselves bangs). To keep them out of trouble and thoroughly entertained, we’ve rounded up some awesome games for toddlers that are sure to be a hit, whether you’re indoors or outdoors. The best part? Your kiddo won’t know it, but they offer ample opportunities for hands-on learning. Ready for endless fun? On your mark. Get set. Go find your tot’s newly introduced fave!

Toddlers are bundles of energy: always on the move, always growing, always learning. Learning with play is essential for their development because it improves small and large motor skills, muscle strength, emotional intelligence, language development, spatial awareness, and more. According to an article by Michael Yogman, MD, FAAP, on Healthychildren.org, “research shows play can improve children’s abilities to blueprint, organize, get along with others, and regulate emotions. In addition, play helps with language, math, and social skills, and even helps children cope with stress.”.

It has been revealed that figuring out how to keep toddlers engaged is no easy feat. There are outdoor games, indoor games, toys, beginner board games… You get the idea. The key is to decide which activity is right for your kiddo, and that depends on factors like their age, energy level, developmental stage, and other milestones.

One of the most important things to consider is what interests your toddler. Do they love Ms. Rachel? Are they obsessed with a sport? Do they love baby dolls or animals? Once you figure out what will keep them interested, you can go from there.

Another factor is something called Play Schemas, a concept first used by Swiss psychologist Jean Piaget. As stated in My Play Cupboard, Play Schemas are repeated patterns of behaviour you notice children engaging in when they play. Nine schemas can be commonly observed in young children, including connection, transforming, enveloping, enclosing, and positioning.

Once you figure out which Play Schema your toddler is drawn to, that will help you decide what type of games they’ll enjoy the most.

It has been revealed that give your jumping bean something to jump about—letters! We love that this outdoor game from The Imagination Tree combines alphabet awareness with the chance to get those wiggles out. Simply write letters in sidewalk chalk and have your little one hop from one to another as you call them out. And all you need to get started is a set of sidewalk chalk. Read all about it and check out the phonics and math variations over at The Imagination Tree.

Let your toddler be your boss with a few rounds of Simon Notes. Toddlers love the chance to be in charge! Then, you can give the commands for a bit. It's silly, active, and engaging—that's why it's an early childhood classic. Plus, it gives little ones a chance to practice following instructions, taking turns, and building listening skills. Simon Says go play!

Sources indicate that toddlers love climbing under, over, and on top of all sorts of things. Obstacle courses let you take that natural climbing instinct and make it a game. Build an indoor obstacle course with painters' tape, making lines for your little one to walk on top of and jump over. Or take the fun outside and challenge them to stay off the grass in the yard or the wood chips at the playground. Ready for a bonus round? Turn the obstacle course game into follow-the-leader and take turns being the leader. Check out this post for even more obstacle course fun.

When you're playing with younger toddlers, change it to the animal sounds game: make a sound (MOOO!) and have the toddler guess what kind of animal makes that noise. What are the benefits of toddler games?

Playing games with your toddler is not only a great opportunity to enjoy quality time with your child, but they help develop crucial life skills like problem solving, small and large motor skills, physical coordination, hand-eye coordination, and learning how to be social with others.

What types of games are best for toddlers?

In a recent development, while it depends on your child’s age, interests, and development, the best toddler games are simple and fun. Popular ideas include pretend play, memory games, music games, and basic movements, like a simplified version of Simon States.

How much screen time is appropriate for toddlers?

According to the American Academy of Child & Adolescent Psychiatry, toddlers should have very limited daily screen time.

There are online toddler games that are designed specifically for young children. Parents should always review the game or content before allowing their child to watch, monitor usage, and opt for an ad-free, child-friendly tablet or platform.

What are some fun indoor games for toddlers?

Toddler indoor games should be fun and easy to set up: memory, obstacle courses, block building challenges, sensory stations, and pretend play like “the floor is lava,” “vet clinic,” and “grocery store.”.

#205188. Why You Should Fight the Urge to Make a Happy Kid Happier
