What Gut Health Actually Means, In A World Where The Algorithm Is Constantly Shilling Supplements

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1130 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scarymommy

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Here’s what experts actually look for, recommend, and see as red flags.
  • In a recent development, nervous system regulation, sleepmaxxing, high-functioning burnout — there is always some hot new health topic du jour.
  • We’ve heard the term; what does it actually mean?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here’s what experts actually look for, recommend, and see as red flags.

In a recent development, nervous system regulation, sleepmaxxing, high-functioning burnout — there is always some hot new health topic du jour. While there’s usually some kernel of true health information buried in the hype, it’s hard to parse what really matters from all the social media “gurus” shilling supplements at the link in bio. This is especially true of “gut health,” a topic that feels like it has dominated wellness spaces for the past few years but also never really comes up in your primary care doctor’s office. So, what does gut health actually mean, particularly for women? What do we need to know, and what is social media fluff?

We’ve heard the term; what does it actually mean? In general, gut health refers to the state of your gastrointestinal tract and how it’s working for you, according to the American Medical Association (AMA). Regular bowel movements, no persistent pain or bloating — these are signs things are going well. Medically speaking, good gut health doesn’t mean you’ve somehow optimized your microbiome (more on that in a minute); it means your digestive tract is functioning as it should, you’re absorbing the nutrients you need, and you’re comfortable throughout the process.

In a recent development, “I think that it looks different for everybody, but when I have a healthy gut, I feel better overall in my day-to-day life. It’s no bloating on a consistent basis. It’s having regular bowel movements. I’m not racing to the bathroom with loose stools or, on the other side of it, I’m not going days constipated. I don’t feel that brain fog. I have energy, and I’m sleeping well,” indicates Chloe Melas, NBC News correspondent and author of The Girl’s Guide to Guts, who lives with ulcerative colitis, a type of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD).

Yes, it is a real thing and the subject of reams of medical research.

Inside your intestines live trillions of microorganisms that have a surprising impact on our overall health. According to The Cleveland Clinic, they help break down our food, support our immune systems, and may even play a role in mood and behavioral health. There’s no one perfect gut microbiome either, according to the AMA. Each person’s is unique and depends on their age, diet, medications, genetics, where they live, and more.

It’s normal to have an off tummy day every now and then, sure, but from her own experience and speaking with experts while writing her book, Melas knows there are certain red flags women should watch for when it comes to their gut health.

Recent findings suggest that “If you’re having blood in your stool on a consistent basis, and that more than a handful of times, you need to go see a doctor immediately. That can look like going to see your primary care. Personally, in my experiences in writing this book and interviewing so many different experts, and just what I've gone through in my own life having IBD, I’d say go straight to a gastroenterologist,” Melas claims.

Sources indicate that vomiting, unexplained weight loss, chronic stomach pain, and difficulty swallowing are also red flags, per the AMA. Inconsistent bowel movements, whether that means racing to the bathroom multiple times a day or being chronically constipated, are another reason to schedule an appointment with your doctor, she adds. Cramping, painful bloating, or looking pregnant after eating a meal — these things are not normal, states Melas.

Industry observers note that ignoring early signs of GI issues can keep you from feeling your best, and in some cases, missing a diagnosis you need. Women are twice as likely as men to have IBS, according to the American College of Gastroenterology.

“For so long, so many of us have just sort of been like, ‘This is just the way life is.’ I think that as women, we just don’t prioritize our health like we should, especially when it comes to our gut health. We’re really good about getting our mammograms and talking about our breast health. We are now finally talking about perimenopause and those symptoms. But 45 million Americans suffer from IBS. Nearly 4 million Americans suffer from inflammatory bowel disease, which raises your chances of having colon cancer. And these are things that require a doctor to help you diagnose.”.

Probiotic sodas, gummies, powders... what do experts say will actually help improve your GI health and comfort? What will actually make your microbiome happy, and what’s not worth the money? Health experts agree that a diet rich in fiber is the best way to support your gut’s health.

It has been revealed that “I had the privilege of interviewing Dr. William Lee, and he wrote a famous book called Eat to Beat Disease. He said that you have 39 trillion different bacteria that live inside your microbiome and that you need this gut diversity to have overall good health, and that it really just comes down to having a diverse plate every day when you’re sitting down for your meals,” Melas states.

It has been revealed that it’s generally recommended for adults to consume 25 to 30 grams of fiber per day, which Melas admits can be hard sometimes with diet alone. That may mean a fiber supplement is worth the investment for you, or it may mean snacking on more fruits and veggies throughout the day where you can.

“We all get so overwhelmed; we’re constantly being targeted by drink this, eat that, take this supplement, take these vitamins. But Dr. Lee notes that really what you need is in the front of the grocery store. It's the fruits, it's the vegetables, and that it's the things that are easiest to reach first,” Melas adds.

Ultimately, Melas claims she wants more women to prioritize their health, and not to be embarrassed or afraid to talk to their providers about GI health specifically.

Recent findings suggest that “If you are not having regular bowel movements, and by that I mean a big, beautiful, healthy poop every single day, then something is off with your gut health, full stop, and you need to get it figured out,” she says. “If you are bloated all the time, if you feel like every time you eat that cheese or a certain meal that you all of a sudden look like you’re three months pregnant, you’re not imagining it and you’re not crazy. We’ve just been told for so long to normalize it, and it's embarrassing, and it's not sexy, and who wants to sit around with your girlfriends at night and talk about the consistency of your stools? But we need to be talking about it because, honestly, it could save lives.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Are parents doomed to a lifetime of chasing after good sleep?

Sources indicate that on a tip from a savvy movie critic, I took my 7-year-old out to see his second ever Marvel movie the other day (he's a big fan of Norse mythology so he's seen Thor: Ragnarok and sorta liked it). We sat back, donning our 3D glasses (he was very into the novelty of this) and took in The Fantastic Four: First Steps. What a pleasant surprise. The movie is, in fact, as my movie critic colleague promised, The Best Marvel Movie for Families.

Industry observers note that for the kids, there’s a lot to love. There are the action montages, a bright retro futuristic setting, a visual style that is gee-whiz superhero cool, but in a comic way — shiny and light and not over the top. The movie is just more palatable for kids than most other Marvel movies, emotionally and cognitively. The superheroes are relatable as family but they also play the part of role models well, interacting with and caring deeply about the public they serve. The villain, too, is not so much motivated by evil but by an unstoppable appetite (for planets, granted) that he is actively trying to rid himself of. A little sympathy goes a long way to take the teeth out of a monster. But most importantly there’s Franklin, the baby.

The Fantastic Four are a family and have arguments and challenges that are familiar to all kids. One significant one is the strain (and joys) that having a baby puts on, well, everyone. I especially loved seeing Reed Richards and Sue Storm, superheroes with doctorates who no doubt have seen their share of sleep debt, complain about tiredness. Even genius superheroes can’t face the superheroic task that is getting baby to bed. It’s a tension that gets the screen time it deserves. Just ask any parent.

Recent findings suggest that sleep has been on my mind a lot lately. I always thought that I would crush sleep once my baby grew up, but some 6 years later I realize maybe it wasn’t the baby? I’ve never met someone who doesn’t have a tenuous relationship with sleep. When I was in physical prime either during my senior high school years as a soccer player and middle distant runner or during my marathon-happy thirties, I slept so very soundly. At least that’s how I remember it.

According to recent reports, now that I’m older I juggle more — so much more — work out a little less and do a lot more staring at the ceiling in the middle of the night. With age, I maybe need to admit, I need an assist.

I’ve only just started to give sleep tracking a fair shake. I’ve been pairing up a newly introduced Samsung Galaxy 8 watch with a Samsung Galaxy Ring (I’ve been a Samsung man since I converted to their Flip phone, which pairs seamlessly together, requiring no third-party apps).

Recent findings suggest that so what have I found? That data is in fact motivating. I won’t get too into the weeds but I will tell you that late night snacks, screens, night caps, and work are bad for my sleep. Evening walks, reading, and days with lighter fare and more quality workouts lead to more quality sleep.

In a recent development, it’s all fairly obvious stuff, but what the tracking does is force the attention. Good sleep matters and is, for those of us without babies, a fairly controllable thing. We can create habits that help sleep. We can choose to prioritize our health and well being. Stats don’t tell us what to do, but they do show what our current priorities.

It has been revealed that when my son was a sleepless baby (he really was the worst) the only two priorities I had were to keep him healthy (alive) and to find sleep. My world is a little easier now and my list of priorities has grown immensely. I want to be outdoors more, to find new fitness, to take on new passions (birding is kind of fun, everyone), to embrace a new phase of marriage, to learn new skills, and meet my kids where they are. But sometimes you have to remember the basics. Without good sleep, everything is more difficult. Only a superhero can defeat the eater of worlds on a new parent’s sleep schedule. The rest of us need all the help we can get.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You can’t germ-proof your kid, but a pediatrician notes these three habits get you pretty close.

According to recent reports, most parents can relate to the joyous feeling of their child(ren) finally returning to school after summer break and, by mid-fall, (hopefully) hitting that back-to-school-routine stride. And conversely, the underlying anxiety of knowing it’s only a matter of time before they get sick and have to stay home. It’s a question worth asking: Is there anything we can do to prevent our kids from being a petri dish at school? I spoke with Dr. Brittany Odom, a board-certified pediatrician, mom, and trusted pediatric health educator, to see if she had any useful advice on preventing the many, many illnesses our children pick up this time of year.

“There are definitely some things we can do to prevent our kids from getting sick, but it is impossible to totally prevent it. So, them getting sick is not a parenting fail,” Dr. Odom wants to first point out. She then highlighted three ways we can take action against these seasonal illnesses.

Recent findings suggest that A landing routine is what your kids do the moment they walk into your house after school. Kind of like stop, drop, and roll, minus the roll. Have them immediately remove any items from school, like their jackets, backpacks, and shoes.

Sources indicate that then, kids should wash their hands. “That way, we are not tracking all of the germs from school throughout the house,” she explains. Furthermore, this is even more important for families with babies at home because “older siblings bringing illnesses home is one of the most common ways babies get sick.”.

“Your eyes, nose, and mouth create your T-zone, and this area is where a lot of germs can enter our bodies,” shares Odom. So simply emphasizing to our children to keep their hands away from this area is majorly helpful. Furthermore, if kids are apt to touch the T-zone regardless of what you say, enforcing handwashing is obvious, but worth stating again. “Washing hands at the most important times is helpful too. So, before we eat, after we use the bathroom, and before touching a baby sibling.”.

If we can also teach kids to cough and sneeze into their elbow instead of their hands, that’s one more way to prevent the germs from entering the T-zone.

Sources indicate that “Have a basket already set up with everything you need at 2 a.m. when your kid wakes up with a fever and they’re feeling terrible,” Odom recommends. These are the products Odom suggests having in there, and luckily, they are all easily shoppable in stores and online:.

Industry observers note that beyond these three tips, Odom recommends that all children ages 6 months and older get both the flu and COVID vaccine. (Mom tip: An easy option for accomplishing this is CVS’s MinuteClinic, which is faster and oftentimes more convenient than a trip to the doctor’s office.).

According to recent reports, additionally, if you have an infant under 8 months old entering their first RSV season, and you did not receive the maternal RSV vaccine during pregnancy, talk to your pediatrician about getting this one too. It's also approved for babies 8 months to 19 months old who are considered "high risk.”.

Industry observers note that “Send your kids back when they are fever-free for at least 24 hours and symptoms have dramatically improved,” says Odom. As much as we want them out the next day, sending them back sick is harmful and disruptive to other students. And you don’t want to be that mom!

Industry observers note that since typical cold care medicines aren’t recommended for children under 4 years old, Odom claims to focus on “supportive care.” These are ways to bring them some comfort and relief from their symptoms. Non-medicated saline sprays are useful, as well as a nasal aspirator. “There’s a lot of watchful waiting, making sure they are feeding well, still giving you wet diapers, and staying hydrated,” shares Odom. A humidifier is also helpful: “I recommend a cool-mist rather than warm-mist humidifier. It should be emptied and cleaned regularly to prevent mold or bacterial growth.”.

In a recent development, taking Odom’s words to heart, I tried to institute a landing routine today when my 3-year-old returned home from preschool. Sure, he said “no” when I asked him to wash his hands. But then, with the promise of some lollipops, he reconsidered. Hands washed, he immediately ran to my 6-month-old in her bouncer. And yes, he went for her T-zone, but hey, at least his hands were clean. I’ll take the win!

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

How should we all tackle phone use and screen time? An ancient Eleusinian mystery may hold the answer.

Does anyone have a truly healthy relationship with their phone?

I don’t see much evidence of it out there. Personally, the phone is undeniably useful but still feels like a foreign object in my hand — a feeling that was brought into stark relief the second my kids were old enough to pick up a screen. To them, a tablet or phone offers an enticing, comforting, and even productive space. Not healthy, exactly, but familiar. For me, it’s alien — and ground zero for a cultural battle against brain rot, attention loss, and reality itself. Phones stress me out.

I ran into a much needed perspective on this dilemma in a long, thoughtful essay by Karl Ove Knausgaard, the brilliant Norwegian writer with an uncanny ability to see the world as it is, in meticulous detail. My struggle, as he helped me to see, comes from those most influential years in my life — the years before the smartphone. “To understand a man, you have to know what was happening in the world when he was twenty, Napoleon is supposed to have said,” writes Knausgaard in Harper’s Magazine. “The quotation is probably apocryphal, but that doesn’t mean it’s not true.”.

It has been revealed that my Napoleonic prime was in the 2000s — shortly after the advent of Facebook, but right before the iPhone was in everyone’s hands. For Knausgaard, who is 56 years old, the internet barely existed in his twenties. He admits that he has been ignoring the fundamental influences of such technological advances since. “Not once in those forty years have I turned my attention to technology and tried to understand it,” Knausgaard writes, “how it works in itself, how it works in me. It’s as if I had moved to a foreign country and not bothered to learn its language, as if I am content with not understanding what is happening around me and just settling for my own little world. This lately feels like serious neglect.”.

This resonates. While I spend considerable time trying to understand and control the impacts of screen time on my kids' developing brains, I hardly pay attention to my own use. What am I doing when I check for emails, Slack messages, and texts with lab rat-like repetition, or scroll Reddit News and The Newly introduced York Times at every down moment, or get lost in Instagram and YouTube rabbit holes? More importantly, what should I do about it?

According to recent reports, knausgaard found his technological insight by heading out to Athens, Greece to talk to James Bridle, an author and artist with a specialty in nonhuman ways of thinking (and what orangutans can teach us about politics). In a sense, Bridle sees technology as getting in the way of experience. Sounding like a free range parenting proselytizer, he says that “the only thing you can do is experience it and do it yourself. You have to do it, you have to experience it, it has to happen to you. Bodily, physically — because you’re part of the world.”.

Bridle takes this deeper, offering the example of an ancient Eleusinian cult in which initiates were led into a dark room, shown a “whirlwind of impressions, without anyone telling them what they were seeing or what it meant” and being left to interpret that on their own. The next year, they were shown the initiation from the outside, “and you could say that only then, when the gaze from within was complemented by the gaze from without, was the initiation completed.”.

This metaphor for the digital world made it all click for me. We’re all too often inside looking at the whirlwind of the internet with little control and understanding. There are more of us now trying to step outside of this world — to see the puppet masters at play in order to walk away from it all.

Industry observers note that we’re not going back to 2006, that innocent year before the iPhone was introduced. And I don’t think that should be the goal. The technology that has been introduced since my childhood is incredible, powerful, and a substantial piece of human progress. But it’s no replacement for the real world lessons I get when I put down the phone and experience life, unfiltered.

#205122. What 28 Years Later Can Tell Us About Men Today

What 28 Years Later Can Tell Us About Men Today

📅 11 Sep 2025 | ⏱️ 3 min read (617 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Danny Boyle’s zombie trilogy is a timely and important meditation about masculinity.
  • Will it take a zombie apocalypse to fix masculinity?
  • Recent findings suggest that I won’t spoil too much in the way of the plot but I will say that the way the story speaks to masculinity — wading through lost men, toxic lies, and not-so-symbolic alpha males (in the form of one truly terrifying zombie) — is thoughtful and fresh.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Danny Boyle’s zombie trilogy is a timely and important meditation about masculinity.

Will it take a zombie apocalypse to fix masculinity? The thought occurred to me as I sat in a theater taking in Danny Boyle’s 28 Years Later the other day. This intense, gory, nudity-laden flick was also one of a surprisingly heartwarming journey for a young boy, Spike, who doesn’t buy into his community’s view of the world. Everyone around him is fearful, incurious, and readily accepts convenient and clear falsehoods about their lives. Spike seeks hope, even if it requires him to face the violent, cruel, and potentially fatal real world off his island.

Recent findings suggest that I won’t spoil too much in the way of the plot but I will say that the way the story speaks to masculinity — wading through lost men, toxic lies, and not-so-symbolic alpha males (in the form of one truly terrifying zombie) — is thoughtful and fresh. In context of the cultural landscape for boys and men today, it’s the kind of exploration we could really use.

Two months ago, Scott Galloway, a professor of marketing at NYU and media tour de force affectionately known on his podcast as Prof G, took to The View to talk, as he does so often, about masculinity.

“I like the idea of restoring an aspirational vision of masculinity,” he stated to a room that seemed, a bit surprisingly, in total agreement. “I don’t think there’s anything wrong with leaning into your femininity or masculinity if it feels natural.”.

In his view, this vision of masculinity involves three pillars: provider, procreator, and protector.

In 28 Years Later, Spike becomes the provider, chasing the health care his mom needs that his dad ignores.

Industry observers note that when it comes to the provider, “every man at the outset of his career should take economic responsibility for his household. Sometimes that means getting out of the way” of your more successful partner, he says, and other times it means stepping up. For procreation, he says we should channel “that fire of desire… the right ways [to] make you a better man — kinder, stronger, thinking about how you dress … showering, for God’s sake.”.

In a recent development, finally, he notes that in an aspirational vision of masculinity, “your default operating system is protection.” This is a more gentle and empathetic pillar than it might sound on its face. “A lot of women don’t feel safe on the subway,” he explains, “or they see men walking down the street, they cross the sidewalk.” This is due to men eschewing their duty as protector. And “it’s not just physical,” he continues. “When you see a group being demonized, your default setting as a man is you move to protection.”.

In 28 Years Later, Spike found himself chasing this view of masculinity headlong: providing the health care his mom needed that his dad would not, protecting her from zombies and himself from indoctrination, not exactly chasing procreation (he’s 12) but rejecting his father’s philandering example. The fact that he lives in a post-apocalyptic landscape in many senses brings clarity to his vision. When there are no worldly comforts, moral clarity arises.

Danny Boyle and Prof G have this in common: They’re both speaking to the broadest possible audiences about things that so many men primarily discuss with, well, other men. With 28 Years Later raking in over $100 million at the box office already and The View’s audience being, well, The View’s audience, it’s refreshing to see such discussion spilling out into the public.

It has been revealed that masculinity is making a comeback. It’s time to talk about it.

Yes, My Toddler Sleeps In Our Room. No, We Haven't Stopped Having Sex.

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1180 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scarymommy

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Before you judge me, I asked experts what young kids actually understand and if our obsession with sexual privacy is more cultural and modern than we think.
  • It has been revealed that my 3-year-old still sleeps in bed with my husband and me.
  • Sources indicate that to which I say: We manage just fine, thanks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Before you judge me, I asked experts what young kids actually understand and if our obsession with sexual privacy is more cultural and modern than we think.

It has been revealed that my 3-year-old still sleeps in bed with my husband and me. I like cuddling him all night, and I’ve come to accept that it’s just the kind of mom I am: the clingy co-sleeping type. When he was littler, we took safe-sleep precautions with a bassinet and all that jazz, but these days, he sleeps right up next to me. Most non-co-sleeping families cringe at this. And then they immediately want to know: So how do you get intimate with your partner?

Sources indicate that to which I say: We manage just fine, thanks. But lately, I’ve been wondering about the elephant in the room. Or, should I say, the toddler.

Recent findings suggest that my husband and I NEVER have sex in the bed with our toddler. But we do sneak into the bathroom. Or sometimes, once he’s deeply asleep, we pull out a cot on the other side of the room and get it on in the dark. I’m embarrassed even admitting that.

I also don’t believe we’re the only parents who have ever found themselves in this predicament.

Here’s the thing... our house isn’t huge. And between the 3-year-old sleeping soundly in our blacked-out bedroom and one of our much more aware older kids wandering out of their rooms, we’ve chosen the former.

Sources indicate that which brings me to something else we really need to address. What about the “olden days”? Ma and Pa from Little House on the Prairie managed to have four babies while living in one-room log cabins and shanties. I guarantee they weren’t heading out to the barn or the outhouse every time they wanted to have sex, especially when bears and wolves were roaming around, and temperatures dipped below zero.

Besides, many modern families around the world still live and sleep in shared spaces.

Lately I’ve wondered if being horrified by the idea of parents having sex in the same room as a sleeping child is a cultural thing. Is it so awful if they’re still very little? At what point does “they have no idea what’s happening” turn into “Mom and Dad need to find somewhere else to do this”?

We reached out to experts to answer all the questions you’ve probably been dying to know but have been way too embarrassed to ask.

Here’s the short answer: Parents don’t need to feel guilty about having sex in the same room as a newborn or young infant. An infant doesn’t have the “cognitive capacity to understand what sex is,” and they won’t remember or understand what’s going on, claims Kimberly Resnick Anderson, LCSW, an AASECT-certified sex therapist.

Anderson does add one caveat, though. Having a baby nearby is likely to make parents more reserved and overall less expressive during sex. Over time, she claims, that could potentially lead to a “more permanent shift” in how they express themselves sexually.

When does she recommend finding some privacy? Around age 1.

Once a child develops language and becomes mobile, she says, it becomes harder to get it on, knowing the child could wake up in the middle of it.

But Samantha Ridout, M.Phil., BCBA, a child development and behavioral expert, cautions against treating any birthday as a universal cutoff. No two children develop at exactly the same rate, she says, so there isn’t a magical age when a child suddenly becomes aware of what’s happening around them. Instead, parents should watch for their child’s growing alertness and awareness and set appropriate boundaries.

I’ve found this to be true in my own family. We moved our older two kids out of our room quicker because they were definitely more aware than our last, who just feels more “babyish.”.

But both experts made one thing very clear: During sex, infants need to be in a separate, safe sleep space.

Let’s go back to my Ma and Pa observation for a minute, shall we?

According to recent reports, the idea of children and adults having separate bedrooms is a relatively upcoming phenomenon, states Macall Gordon, a researcher and sleep coach with an undergraduate degree in anthropology who studies children’s sleep through a sociohistorical lens. She says before the lightbulb was invented, family life revolved around sunrise and sunset, with families often sleeping in shared spaces.

Recent findings suggest that but with electricity, adults could suddenly stay up after children went to bed, she adds. Now, children needed a “separate space to sleep” while adults stayed up. So the nursery and the crib came along. Then, she indicates, the layout of homes started to change, too, to include hallways connecting separate rooms. Before that, rooms were all connected to each other, so you had to go through one to get to another.

To this day, however, a separate bedroom is still something of a privilege. Many families simply don’t have “extra, separate rooms,” Gordon points out, especially in big cities, where studios and lofts are common, or in cultures where extended family members may occupy additional bedrooms. “While we think of a separate room for children as the norm, it really wasn’t for most of our history,” Gordon shares.

Industry observers note that tiffany Belanger, cosleeping expert and founder of Cosleepy, states the topic tends to divide her followers into two camps: those who will have sex in the room with a kid and those who won’t. When I described my scenario to her, she responded that floor sex while young kids are still sleeping in their parents’ bed is actually pretty common among the co-sleeping families she hears from.

You want to know if mine has woken up before.

But rarely. He’s a really deep sleeper, and it’s only happened a few times. It’s dark, and when he did wake up, he immediately called out for me in that disoriented, half-asleep way toddlers do. We stopped immediately. The cot is also on the far side of the bed, outside his line of sight. As far as I know, he never saw or heard anything.

Sources indicate that will we emotionally damage our kid if he were to catch us in the act? Unlikely, Ridout claims, if parents stay calm, stop immediately, tell the child they are safe, and answer their questions in a simple, non-panicky way.

But all of this still leaves me with the extremely practical question that got us into this mess in the first place.

Parents have to get creative, flexible, and spontaneous, states Anderson. That might mean asking family or friends to babysit when you can, doing it in other rooms, or using whatever short pockets of privacy you can find.

And while Belanger reassures me that my floor-sex solution isn't unheard of among co-sleeping parents, the other experts think it’s not a great option when kids become mobile and verbal. So, I suppose it might be time to retire the cot. Where to next?

How To Make Fewer Grocery Trips & Still Eat Well

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1372 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scarymommy

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Groceries cost a fortune, gas isn’t cheap… every “quick” run to the store somehow costs you 60 bucks or more.
  • In a recent development, it’s a phenomenon that happens more often than not these days: You run into the store for milk, cheese, eggs, and a few other basics, and walk out wondering how in the hell a small handful of grocery bags just set you back upwards of 100 bucks.
  • The reality is groceries are still painfully expensive, and plenty of families are stretched thinner than ever.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Groceries cost a fortune, gas isn’t cheap… every “quick” run to the store somehow costs you 60 bucks or more. Experts share how to shop less and still feed your family well.

In a recent development, it’s a phenomenon that happens more often than not these days: You run into the store for milk, cheese, eggs, and a few other basics, and walk out wondering how in the hell a small handful of grocery bags just set you back upwards of 100 bucks. Worse, you then have to play budget Tetris, moving money around to make sure you have funds for the inevitable grocery run you’ll have to make next week. Add in the gas it takes to get to and from, and you’re spent literally and figuratively.

The reality is groceries are still painfully expensive, and plenty of families are stretched thinner than ever. And, sure, cutting back on trips is probably one of the easiest and most logical ways to save money (and time, and sanity). But it begs the question: How long can you go between grocery runs without your family surviving on cereal benders?

We asked food and budgeting experts how they personally make it work.

Recent findings suggest that most of the experts we polled noted one substantial shop a week is sort of the sweet spot. “Every extra trip not only takes up valuable time, but is also another chance to grab things that aren’t on the list and drive up your overall grocery bill,” states Laurie Hise, CEO of Passionate Penny Pincher.

It has been revealed that is it possible to stretch it to every two weeks? Maybe. But AJ Prasaguet, head of the iconic Palace bar and restaurant in Miami Beach, points out that biweekly shopping “can work if you have the storage space, freezer capacity, and money available upfront. Those are real considerations, and not every household has all three.”.

According to recent reports, amber Hanson, a licensed nutritionist and founder of Whole You Nutrition, emphasizes that there’s no cut-and-dry, one-size-fits-all answer. Your ideal grocery-shopping cadence will ultimately depend on things like how close you live to a store and when your paycheck hits the bank. If you get paid every two weeks, it might make sense to shop on that timeframe too.

Sources indicate that before you make your little grocery list and head to the store, open up your own fridge, freezer, and pantry. “The best way to save money is to use what you have already paid for,” notes Hanson.

Industry observers note that jenn Lueke, New York Times-bestselling author of Don’t Think About Dinner, does her inventory every Friday night, then builds the next week’s meals around what’s left. Example: “If I know I have a half carton of broth that needs to be used, I’ll make sure to pick up a grain, like rice or quinoa, that I can cook in it.”.

Sources indicate that prasaguet goes one step further. “Give an ingredient its next job before you buy it. If a recipe needs half a container of something, decide where the other half is going.” Take cabbage, for instance. It can be slaw one night, stir-fry the next, and soup filler after that.

In a recent development, another tip Hise is a fan of is ordering online for pickup or delivery when you can. The simple act of skipping the aisles means you don't have to worry about impulse buys wreaking havoc on your total.

Industry observers note that as a busy working mom who regularly feels she has to have everything for the week figured out at all times, this was very liberating to hear! As the experts remind us, life happens. Plans change. A rigid seven-night menu is a fast track to wasted food.

But if it makes you feel better to have the week mostly lined up, you could follow Hise’s example: proposal five “fresh” dinners a week, leaving one night for leftovers and one for a meal pulled from what’s already in the pantry, fridge, or freezer. Prasaguet relies on a similar formula: four planned dinners, one leftovers meal, one pantry or freezer dinner, on flex night. “That gives the week some structure without pretending everything will go according to plan,” he states.

Lueke recommends starting with dinners, then exploring how you can make the most of them. “Will the slow-cooker chicken stretch to cover lunches for half the week too? Can I make a double batch of quinoa and bulk up our mid-week sheet pan dinner?” Theme nights like Taco Tuesday or Breakfast for Dinner also help reduce decision fatigue.

The trick to making groceries last, many of the pros explained, is buying foods with different lifespans and eating them in the right order. “You do not want an entire cart of produce that all needs attention at once,” emphasizes Prasaguet.

Lueke thinks about it in three zones:.

Andrea Woroch, a consumer savings expert, notes that some hardy produce (think garlic, potatoes, sweet potatoes, winter squash, even whole apples) can last for months depending on storage conditions as well as how they’re handled. For fast-spoilers like berries, resist the urge to buy the giant fresh packs unless you know your family will gobble them down. Otherwise, stock up on frozen.

If you're afraid frozen and canned food won't pack the same nutritional punch as fresh, well, the experts beg to differ.

Industry observers note that “One of the biggest misconceptions about healthy eating is that fresh foods are always better than frozen or canned alternatives. That’s simply not the case,” states Jennifer Pallian, a registered dietitian and founder of Foodess. Frozen vegetables are typically flash-frozen shortly after harvest, and research has found they can be just as nutritious as fresh produce that’s been sitting in your fridge for several days. In some cases, they even have more vitamin C.”.

According to recent reports, don’t turn your nose up at canned staples, either. Pallian is a massive proponent of canned light tuna (a solid source of protein, selenium, and omega-3s) and canned chickpeas, which pack both protein and fiber and are already cooked.

Just opt for low-sodium or no-salt-added canned veggies and beans, and be mindful of foods packed in juices, syrups, or sauces.

Adopting a few little habits can go a long way toward making food last until your next grocery run:.

However, Prasaguet reminds us, “Stretching groceries should never mean stretching food safety.” That means refrigerating leftovers within two hours, eating them within three to four days, or sticking them in the freezer.

Sources indicate that you should know that eating well doesn’t mean you have to buy a bunch of fancy superfoods. “Some of the most nutrient-dense foods in the grocery store are also the cheapest,” Hanson indicates.

Here’s what our experts say they keep stocked:.

And while many of us think shopping in bulk must save money, Prasaguet notes that it’s “only better value if you can afford it, store it, and finish it.” Hise’s workaround is to grab a few extra cans whenever they’re on sale. “A few extra cans a month can add up to a pantry that carries you through a tight month.”.

If you feel like a failure every time you serve your family dinner out of a bag or can, it’s high time you cut yourself some slack.

Sources indicate that “Frozen and canned foods that you actually eat beat fresh vegetables you throw away every time,” says Hise. Link agrees, adding, “I’d much rather see a family use convenient foods they enjoy than buy fresh ingredients that become a science experiment in the crisper drawer.”.

Industry observers note that “A fed family is a win, and ‘fresh’ isn’t the measure of a good dinner," Lueke puts it simply. A balanced meal is made up of a protein, a plant or two, and something filling. It truly does not matter if those came from the produce section or the freezer aisle.

Industry observers note that but maybe Prasaguet sums it up best. “You do not have to prove your love through a complicated dinner,” he reassures. “Feeding your family with the resources you have is already an act of care.”.

#205116. Are Our Chidlren Really So Mentally Unwell?

Are Our Chidlren Really So Mentally Unwell?

📅 01 Dec 2025 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2766 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • American kids are having a mental health crisis like no other.
  • According to recent reports, in a Fresh York Time ideas story that ran this past week, Jia Lynn Yang opens with a bang: “One of the more bewildering aspects of the already high-stress endeavor of 21st-century American parenting is that at some point your child is likely to be identified with a psychiatric diagnosis of one kind or another.
  • For those with tweens and teens, this might seem obvious.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

American kids are having a mental health crisis like no other. What are we to do with all these diagnoses?

According to recent reports, in a Fresh York Time ideas story that ran this past week, Jia Lynn Yang opens with a bang: “One of the more bewildering aspects of the already high-stress endeavor of 21st-century American parenting is that at some point your child is likely to be identified with a psychiatric diagnosis of one kind or another. Many exist in a gray zone that previous generations of parents never encountered.”.

For those with tweens and teens, this might seem obvious. For those with younger ones, buckle up.

Sources indicate that in Yang’s story, she focuses on the role schools play. Failures in education may lead to an increase of psychiatric diagnoses like ADHD — alongside IEPs or maybe medications — as a means to catch up kids who are being lost in crowded, test-reliant, merit-funded schools. Of course, even Yang points out that schools are only one part of the puzzle. There’s screens and social media taking over our emotional lives and psychiatric development; the pandemic’s long-felt chilling effect on socialization; the adult world of division and anger in politics and everywhere else; and of course changes within the Mental Health Industrial Complex.

According to recent reports, it’s this last piece that Dr. Sami Timimi, a child and adolescent psychiatrist and psychotherapist at the National Health Service in the United Kingdom is focused on. He's the author of six books including Naughty Boys: Anti-Social Behavior, ADHD, and the Role of Culture and his most recent book, Searching for Normal, which promises to outline a newly introduced approach to understanding mental health, distress and neurodiversity. There little doubt we could use some advice here — and a bit of demystification around the mental health crises that seems to have taken over childhood.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

I frankly found Searching for Normal to be a difficult book. The science and ideas are very clearly laid out, but you're throwing a lot of stones systemically and culturally that are not often cast. As a layperson and a parent with a house filled with diagnoses, medications, cultural shame, and lots of doubts about our mental health journey, the paralysis you describe feels very close to home. Given all this, I'm wondering, big picture, what is the main takeaway you'd want a parent to walk away with from your book?

Dr. Sami Timimi: It is a difficult read because we have a public narrative that's been around for a while that's really created a mythology around what we think of in terms of mental health and behavioral difference. My main message is that what we are calling psychiatric diagnosis aren't really diagnoses. And be careful where the culture of diagnoses might lead you to, because we have so much evidence now that the way we're approaching mental health has resulted in something called the treatment prevention paradox, where at a population level we're seeing increasing prevalence of mental conditions and mental health diagnoses. At the same time we're seeing an increasing number of people accessing various types of treatments associated with these diagnoses.

According to recent reports, but we're not seeing an improvement in the outcomes. If we saw an improvement in the outcomes, we would expect at least a stabilization and hopefully a reduction in prevalence of certain conditions because they would be being effectively treated. I don't think there's actually much disagreement with this in most of the academic literature on what's going on because mental health does seem to be an outlier compared to we've seen a lot of progress in physical health.

For example, when I was a kid, if I got leukemia, my chances of survival into adulthood was around 20%. Now it's around 80%. So this is what happens when you have approaches that are built on technical knowledge that allows you to understand what's going on and make specific treatments for it. But it seems to be the case in mental health that we're going in the wrong direction. What are the assumptions that go missing when we approach mental health as if it's physical health? Because we have to remember, there's no brain scan for ADHD, there's no blood test for anxiety. You can't examine a thought under a microscope. And it becomes difficult to sit in that area of uncertainty and curiosity.

Industry observers note that you talk about the TikTok contagion of health disorders and you cite the, I think it was 2023 research about Canadian teen girls presenting with a variety of self-described disorders that are all relatively rare. I'm wondering if you can describe the phenomenon and then I wonder, what does it change for parents on the ground? We have to take their thoughts seriously, no?

Recent findings suggest that yeah, that's a difficult one, isn't it? It's interesting because I heard about this research from a colleague and friend of mine who's a psychiatrist in Canada who shared this paper and it happened just at the point where I was seeing that in my clinical work as well, I was seeing young people who were brought by their parents, parents very worried, with presentations that are generally considered to be quite rare presentations. So, for example, I saw a number of kids who were coming and saying that they had these Tourette's symptoms but they had no history of it. It's like it suddenly emerged.

In a recent development, it is hard because first of all, I don't blame social media for causing these things because actually a lot of this is narratives that's been suggested and started out. The bigger phenomena are these influencers who say that they have ADHD or autism or anxiety and they publicize it online and they talk about things that are signs of potentially having these conditions. And we have to remember, growing up is tough. Try to remember what I was like as a 13, 14-year-old — it is a struggle. There's a lot of changes going on.

Recent findings suggest that you're in a phase of your life where you're seeking meaning and you're seeking belonging and you're involved in those existential type of scenarios where you're trying to figure out where do I fit in? What's my life all about? And so what's been happening is because they watch a lot of these things online with a lot of the influencers just taking up concepts that have been given to them by certain branches of academic psychiatry. And so what social media is doing is a kind of a social contagion. It's turbocharging these ideas and spreading them out.

This goes alongside a trend that's been happening in parenting.

Recent findings suggest that I think a lot of parents have lost their trust that they know what they're doing. I think a lot of parents have lost their confidence. They feel the need to go to see a professional to try and understand. And it's difficult when a lot of the professionals are also involved in what I call the Mental Health Industrial Complex. This is how they get paid, this is how they earn a living.

And so one of the things that I do encourage parents to do is don't be scared of your children. Don't be scared of their intense emotions and don't be scared of conflict. Conflict happens. What has I think happened as we've exported the knowledge base to professionals is we've also developed a curious form of something that some people refer to as cognitive parenting. I know the concept of helicopter parenting, cognitive parenting is a little bit different where you try to reason things through, where you treat your children as if they're already developed adults.

So what role should parents take?

If you don't think this is good for your children, tell them. If you want to put some boundaries around them, don't be afraid of their conflicts.

Industry observers note that I liken it a little bit to a referee in, well, for us it's a soccer match. Whenever they, say, blow the whistle that there's a foul committed, the offending team that you've blown the whistle for will complain. That's what happens.

According to recent reports, the crowd will complain as well and say the referee is biased and so on. So when you are a rule enforcer, one way to think about it is you're not going to get any good feedback. You're always going to get protests. You have to ride that out. But a good referee delivers the consequence. The consequence is usually fairly short, it's fairly immediate. Don't delay the consequences because you don't say, well, I've seen you doing that foul, but the next match you have, if you do that again, then the next match you have, I'm going to give this or that. Whatever consequence it is, immediate, short-lived, doesn't have to be long. Just something that highlights that you disapprove and this is not allowed.

According to recent reports, and the other thing you do is you don't argue with them. So in soccer matches, you have a half-time where the teams go into the dressing room for 15 minutes before coming. You don't see a referee running after the player who's committed the foul telling them, “I've seen you, I've seen you doing this in other matches. You think you're going to get away with it. You never learn, you never listen.” A good referee spots the infringement, knows that they're going to get back chatted and they're going to get flak, needs to develop a thick skin to ride that out, not rise to it and doesn't get involved in nagging them and so on. And once the consequence is delivered, it's over. Don't need to talk about it again. It's finished.

Recent findings suggest that what happens when you get caught in what you call the Mental Health Industrial Complex? A quote in the book that really resonated with me, asks “What might happen if instead of shaping the treatment around diagnosis, it was put to one side and the specific challenges, fears, and context were engaged with instead?” Can you answer the question you pose? What does that exactly look like?

So one of the things, understanding that what we call psychiatric diagnoses are not actually diagnoses, they're descriptions. They're what a branch of therapy referred to as narrative therapy ...[which] basically indicates that our life is made up of stories. It's the stories we hear about ourselves, the stories others tell about us, and we build up a set of stories to understand ourselves. We're surrounded by narratives. And the narratives we tell ourselves have a powerful impact on how we experience our emotions.

It has been revealed that so what I was describing there is instead of falling down the root of imagining that if you get a diagnosis you found the meaning for what it is that is going on that's troubling you, there is a different way of trying to find out what it is you're trying to achieve, what is it the difference that you're trying to make, that a diagnosis can't do. So one thing I do in my clinical life is a form of what's referred to as Socratic questioning.

Let's say you got a diagnosis and it was the perfect diagnosis and you felt it fitted. What difference do you imagine this is going to make to your life? What difference is that going to make to your life?

It has been revealed that A diagnosis in a sense is an abstract thing. It doesn't really tell you specifically materially what's going on in your world. Is it that actually you're having trouble with friendships? Is it that your family is under stress and you're under stress because you think your parents are about to split up? Is it that you're finding yourself out of your depth at school? So you're trying to get to the specifics of what it is that people are wanting to see change in their life.

Recent findings suggest that right. Keep questioning the outcomes and ideas. I really like this tool for parents.

Industry observers note that and the other thing is I'm trying to help people move past the idea that experiencing intense emotions is a sign that there's something wrong in them. Experiencing intense emotions is something that we all have to go through. If we don't go through it, we have less of a chance to develop psychologically.

In a sense, the role of parents is to be careful about saving your children from struggle and suffering because that is an unrealistic goal. All life involves struggle and suffering at some level. How can we know joy if we don't know sadness? It's impossible.

According to recent reports, you say this is the most pathologized generation ever. Given that, do you have a checklist for parents to look through and say, is my child being pathologized?

That's an interesting question. I may be averse to the whole concept of checklists, partly because in understanding that all our definitions of mental health are subjective. So our understanding of what is and isn't a kind of looming problem that needs some sort of professional intervention. There is no formula that will allow you to figure this one out. It's going to have to be situation, person and family specific.

One thing I say to parents is, look, all good parents feel guilty. That's just a given. I cannot help you with that. Whatever I do, whatever anybody does, you'll carry on feeling guilty or worry, have I done too much of this? Have I interviewed too little? Have I given too much advice? Have I given the wrong? That's what good parents do. Be careful about that guilt driving you to do too much. And I think that's now a bigger danger than the opposite. So we end up intervening perhaps unnecessarily without holding our own anxiety and our own guilt. So one of my little messages is don't try too hard.

On that note, what do you do with the big feelings in a household? How do you let issues not get carried away?

So one of the things that I try to work with with families is understanding, I use the metaphor of a dance, that there's emotional flow going between people and that emotional flow defines how that relationship works. And sometimes what happens is that anger becomes the dominant way in which connection happens.

Industry observers note that the other thing I think about in terms of emotions, I think of emotions as being viral. You catch the emotions of the person closest to you. If your kid is angry with you, it's very hard not to get angry back at them. So kind of developing an awareness of that emotional flow of how it's working in your particular relationship and developing an understanding that that has become a dance.

Sources indicate that for example, I know there was a period in my own kid's life where there was a lot of tension, a lot of sibling rivalry to the point where our son and daughter were getting physical and losing temper. And we thought, me and my wife thought only one of them would survive in childhood. That's what it felt like to us.

Anyway, so I thought, okay, well I have to try and do something about this. So I started writing little post-its at the end of each day, just a few, a sentence or two about things that I liked that happened and I just stuck it above their bed before they went to bed.

After a couple of weeks of doing this, my daughter stated to me, "Dad, you're being weird." And I said, "What do you mean I'm being weird?".

"Why do you keep putting these post-its and saying these nice things?" I mentioned, "Okay, do you like it?".

So just something also a bit playful a bit, but it's just about trying to refine that emotional connection somewhere other than what's become the defining dance.

A little bit of, “all you need is love.” And I think you had it at the top of one of your chapters, quoting Confucius.

It has been revealed that exactly. The journey of a thousand miles starts with the first step.

How To Have A Lazy Thanksgiving Without Losing That Holiday Magic

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1023 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scarymommy

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Delegate the sides, veto the cranberry sauce, and actually sit down at your own table.
  • As a child, I remember the holiday season feeling like the most magical time of the year.
  • According to recent reports, who decorated the house like that?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Delegate the sides, veto the cranberry sauce, and actually sit down at your own table.

As a child, I remember the holiday season feeling like the most magical time of the year. Thanksgiving, in particular, seemed like a substantial deal because it meant Christmas was right around the corner. The house always felt so warm and cozy with fall decorations on full display — their last hurrah before Christmas took over. And the food. There was always so much delicious food to consume. It was wonderful. It was special. And now, as an adult, I realize it was all thanks to... my mom.

According to recent reports, who decorated the house like that? Mom. Who invited the guests and organized the whole Thanksgiving affair? Mom. Who made all of that yummy food? You guessed it — Mom! For me, all of that stuff just seemed to magically get done without much fuss. But there was a fuss. And it wasn’t magic. It was Mom. And now that I’m a mom myself, I realize just how much she had on her plate, figuratively speaking. (Literally, she probably didn’t have much on her plate at all because she was too busy hosting to actually enjoy the meal she created.).

The point is, Thanksgiving can prove to be such a stressful time for moms with all the planning and cooking and putting everyone else’s needs above their own. So much effort is put into making this day perfect for everyone but themselves. But moms deserve to enjoy this holiday too, which is why I say it’s time to invoke a latest tradition known as the Lazy Thanksgiving.

Now I know what you’re thinking, but don’t let the name fool you; a Lazy Thanksgiving doesn’t mean a Lame Thanksgiving. There are still plenty of ways to make this day feel special without completely wiping yourself out in the process. Here’s how.

Recent findings suggest that even if you’re hosting Thanksgiving dinner, that doesn’t mean you should automatically carry the load of the entire meal on your shoulders. Do what any good boss does and delegate an assortment of dishes to other members of the family for them to bring over on the day of. If there’s one thing that you personally enjoy making, then by all means have at it. But everything else should be outsourced to others. Don’t let the burden fall solely on you.

To add a fun twist, reveal that anyone who contributes a dish gets their name entered into a raffle for a special prize at the end of the night. This could be something hassle-free and small, like a cute little ornament or a goodie bag of chocolate. This not only serves as a great incentive to help lighten your cooking load, but it also gives the winner a sweet keepsake of the occasion. (It’s worth noting that this prize part is completely optional — no family member should need to be bribed to help out.).

It has been revealed that if you don’t feel comfortable with a potluck approach, but still feel overwhelmed at the thought of making so many dishes, feel free to just simply not make some of those items. (Think of it as a food-ocracy and you’re the president.) Cranberry sauce may be thought of as a Thanksgiving staple, but if only a spoonful or so gets eaten each year, then you are well within your rights to take it off the menu. The same goes for squash or yams or anything else that never ends up feeling worth the effort you put into making it. Odds are, no one is going to care or miss it, and those who do obtain the right to make it themselves.

Sources indicate that if you really want to unburden yourself and maximize your relaxation time, you could always get the food from somewhere else and either pick it up or have it delivered right to your door. Honey Baked is always a solid option with great choices for a delicious holiday feast.

Sources indicate that it’s more expensive than making it yourself, but a lot less time-consuming, and if various family members chip in to make it happen, it could end up being more than worth the cost. That way you can sit down and actually have time to enjoy everyone’s manufacturer for a change.

Do you enjoy cooking but dread the massive clean-up job that comes at the end of it all? Trade in regular dishes and cups for paper ones. Sure, there will still be some dishes to contend with that the actual food was cooked in, but this swap definitely helps cut down on the task and leaves extra room for everything else to go in the dishwasher.

According to recent reports, as a bonus, you can make use of all the extra paper plates by turning it into a fun craft competition for the kids. Whether they use them to make a snowman or some Thanksgiving-inspired creation, this is a great way to get their artistic juices flowing. Choose a family member to be the judge and give out a prize to the winner each year: something like a small toy or maybe even a NeeDoh if you really want the crowd to go wild and can get your hands on one. The kids will love the challenge and look forward to it as part of an annual tradition.

Then again, do you want to go completely rogue? Throw tradition out the window and order takeout or make an easy casserole that will feed everyone and involve zero stress. No turkey. No stuffing. No gravy. No hassle.

However you choose to invoke your “Lazy Thanksgiving,” just make sure that it’s the right fit for you. The whole point is to put less pressure on this day, and by extension, yourself. Remember that less work for you doesn’t equate to a less enjoyable time for everyone else. You being around more, instead of running back and forth to the kitchen, is something the whole family will be thankful for in the long run.
